I’ve noticed myself not having to use humor as a shield anymore, as much. I’m less afraid to be vulnerable—and not just in my public life but in my personal life too.

Of course, you shouldn’t need the validation of anyone to feel like you’re worthy, but let’s be real.…

What gagged me this year? I would say, honestly, as a statement of ambition, the Javis’ movie [La Bola Negra]. You marvel at it because you’re like, “How the fuck did they pull this off?” To even want to tell that complex of a story, and to just do it and go balls to the wall, is very inspiring.

I was like, “This is too long. It’s embarrassing now.” —A.P.

Jacket and pants by Canali. Shirt by Amiri. Boots by Alessandro Vasini. Tie by Husbands.

Age: 41Breakout moment: Reporting on how the Steve Ballmer–owned Clippers were allegedly funny with money, on his podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out, leading to one of the most severe team penalties in sports history.—————

Two days ago, I walked into this event that The New York Times was holding…it was like the 175th birthday party [for the paper]. I walk out the elevator and literally the first person I see is [NBA commissioner] Adam Silver. I won’t say exactly what he told me, but the tenor of our conversation was like, This is the HBO series adaptation of what this moment would be.

As a first-generation American—my parents are from the Philippines—there’s always been a dream of mine to be cast as a white person. So…Andrew Garfield, come on. Let’s do this.

The funny part is that I’m not even done reporting this story yet. The federal government is now investigating the Clippers, and so I’m now investigating the government’s investigation in the era of Trump too, which is like its own rabbit hole inside of a rabbit hole, which is fucking wild. But at the same time, it feels like now our number is listed in the phone book…actual other NBA owners are calling me up saying, “Can you look into this?”

It’s hard not to be sappy about this, but the lesson I learned is that if you’re telling the truth, you can walk into any room and feel like that as a suit of armor. Even when the person you’re investigating is one of the 10 richest people in the world. —F.T.

Coat by Michael Kors. Vintage pajamas from Palace Costume Co. Socks by London Sock Company. Glasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklaces (throughout), his own.

Age: 37Breakout moments: Stealing scenes as a ’70s Provincetown line cook in the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, and his stand-up special Uncle Stav.—————

I just did The Drew Barrymore Show. That experience was so magical. I was so nervous to be around Drew Barrymore. I’ve done a lot of cool shit, and that’s the one where I was like, “I am actually nervous to the point where I’m not a professional. I’m just a stammering little boy who’s with the girl he had a crush on from The Wedding Singer when he was a fat 10-year-old, and I’m trying to keep it together.”

Last week I allowed myself an aimlessly wander around New York City day. Got a little stoned, walked around, stumbled into a movie. Walked along the water on the West Side. Sat down to a little random omakase. Rode a Citi Bike around. I call it the hero’s journey, where you leave your home at, whatever, 11 a.m. ,with just the bare provisions, and you’re not allowed to go home. You just have to keep moving and keep doing stuff.

I filmed this Judd Apatow movie The Comeback King, with Glen Powell, Cristin Milioti, Madelyn Cline. That comes out in February. I’m excited to do stand-up—for fun, not to explicitly work on another hour. I’m excited to go back to clubs and just like, “Can I be the funniest person in this club tonight?” And that’s my only goal.

To be honest with you, the last three years, it’s [been] all go. But you got to have these big years, or else GQ doesn’t talk to you at the end of the year. —A.P.

On Halkias: Jacket and pants by Brooks Brothers. Shirt by Many. Shoes by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Sunglasses by Valention. On Torre: Jacket by Tom Ford. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shoes by G.H. Bass. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Ring, his own.

Shirts and pants by Dunhill. Underwear by Calvin Klein. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 31Breakout moment: Storming the West Coast rap scene with collabs from Pharrell Williams and Tyler, the Creator on his major-label debut album, No Rest for the Wicked.—————

Not like I made it, but I have arrived. We went to Magic City on a Monday for the first time. They were playing the fuck out my records in that motherfucker. The DJ played “Look Like My Mama” in the strip club. You ain’t never heard Tyler, the Creator get played in a strip club. We crossing worlds that’s never been crossed before.

The day before the album came out, we were in Area 29 in Houston, doing our thing. Regular night, it ain’t too packed, throwing money. They tap me on my shoulder like, “My boy want to holler at you.” They take me upstairs to this private section, pull the curtain back…it’s Travis Scott.

It was epic, bro. N-gga came out from behind the curtain like Batman. The light hid half his face. He said, “I fuck with everything you got going on.” We go back down to that section, 15 minutes pass, then one of the owners came and grabbed me: “Look, look, look.” Travis was up there, playing [Chike’s song] “Packed Up.” —F.T.

Shirt by Lu’u Dan. Pants by Valentino. Bracelet by Cartier.

Age: 26Breakout moment: Being a dead ringer for Sly Stallone in I Play Rocky, the film about…Sly Stallone playing Rocky.—————

In the thick of prep. I was training at Gleason’s Gym with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers. We were beating the crap out of each other and figuring out how to box. I had gained a bunch of weight, and I was trying to actually cut a few pounds, so I was in those sweatsuits, like a garbage-bag type thing. On the way to the gym, I would listen to Stallone and on the way home.… Everything I could find up to 1980, 1985, every piece of Stallone footage that existed.

I [asked] Seth Rogen, “Dude, how do you handle this stuff?” And he said, “Just go with the flow.” It was such a simple answer, but from somebody like him, I was like, He’s got a good grip on this. The simplicity of it landed.

Philip Seymour Hoffman is one. Chadwick Boseman. Christian Bale, Heath Ledger.

[The first Rocky] is the best movie—but when I was younger, the one that caught my eye was four. Rocky IV is nuts. —F.T.

Jacket by Versace. Shirt by 73London. Pants by Umit Benan. Earring (throughout), his own.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: All clothing by Gucci. Shoes by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Brioni. Sunglasses by Ahlem. On Calvo: Jacket, pants, and boots by Tom Ford. Scarf, stylist’s own. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: Jacket and pants by Chanel. Shirt by Factor’s. Shoes by Marsèll. Pin by Cartier. On Calvo: All clothing, tie, and shoes by Ralph Lauren Purple Label. Watch by Cartier.

Ages: Ambrossi, 42 | Calvo, 35Breakout moment: Cowriting and directing La Bola Negra, the gay Spanish historical epic loosely based on an unfinished Federico García Lorca play.——————————————

Javier Ambrossi: Very important. We understood that sometimes people expect LGBTQ+ stories to be niche or for a specific audience. We wanted to do a queer story about universal love.

Ambrossi: It’s a way to put in context how different we are. We change a lot, and the story of our grandparents and our story is very different.

Javier Calvo: What do we do with the freedom our ancestors fought for, and died for?

Calvo: Isabelle Huppert. For me, she’s everything.

Ambrossi: I will go with Julia Roberts. My Best Friend’s Wedding is a very important queer story. The relationship between a woman and a gay man—it was the first time I saw that onscreen. And Rupert Everett was so bold, and I could tell in his eyes that he was gay. I was a kid and I was like, “He’s not faking it.”

How did you celebrate when you won best director at Cannes?

Ambrossi: I put the award on the table and went to sleep. And then Javi came over at 8 a.m.…

Ambrossi: “Give me the award!” And he took it! —A.P.

(from l.) On Ippolito: Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklace by Cartier. On Chike: Shirt and pants by Brioni. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. On Thiele: Jacket by McQueen. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Versace.

#6752. Here’s When Every Episode of ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Drops

Lord of the Rings fans are used to long binges... right? 😰

For many fans, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has been leading up to a lot of the events in season 3, which drops this November on Prime Video. We’re actually gonna see sexy Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forge *that* ring. Now, Peter Jackson turned the war between elves, men, orcs, and more that follows into the prologue of his The Fellowship of the Ring movie...but so much more happened than even his Extended Editions didn’t include. His Galadriel (Cate Blanchett) didn’t even mention relationship history with Sauron. Let this be your guide to the very dark, deceitful, and extraordinarily dramatic third season of The Rings of Power.

Funny I should mention the Extended Editions, actually, because watching the Prime Video series this season is going to feel a lot like settling down for a four-hour film every week. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has decided to release episodes in three “batches” this season. That means that we’ll have multiple episodes to watch every Wednesday, and it’ll be over by December. This is good news for those who have been waiting impatiently for new Middle-earth stories, and terrible news for those of us who like to savor new seasons of television, talk it out with other fans, and experience it together at the same pace. You can’t please everyone!

The premiere is November 11, aka Veterans Day in the United States. And if you haven’t already served, you might feel like you have after binging the four episodes dropping at once on that day. That’s right.

The series is available to watch on Prime Video.

The streamer typically does a midnight release. However, again... let’s think about these batch drops. It might be smarter to log off social media, and wait until the next morning, rather than stay up all night watching the new episodes.

The season will have eight episodes total, just like the two seasons before it. How many episodes will we get each week with this whole batch thing? Like so: four episodes in week 1, two in week 2, and then two in week 3. Got it?

The co-creators J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay alternated writing episodes with writer and producer Justin Noble. Episodes 1, 2, and 8 were directed by Charlotte Brändström, who also directed many episodes in seasons 1 and 2. Episodes 2–4 were directed by Sanaa Hamri, who joined the series in season 2. And episodes 5 and 6 were directed by Stefan Schwartz, who is new to Rings of Power.

#6750. ¡Vamos, España!

With Spain fresh off a World Cup win, there’s no better time to visit Madrid and the cooler northern regions of Asturias and Galicia

I lived in Spain in the early aughts, when the country was experiencing a mic-drop moment. The shiny, futuristic Frank Gehry–designed Guggenheim Museum had gone up in Bilbao a few years earlier, setting off what is now known as the Bilbao effect: a phenomenon that describes how investing in a visionary architecture project can transform a place. Food-obsessed travelers were flocking to a small beach town in a remote corner of northern Spain just to experience a meal at El Bulli, the legendary, now closed, three-Michelin-star restaurant headed up by Ferran Adrià.

Spain is now in the midst of another glow-up, thanks in part to its World Cup win, and Madrid is front and center. A recent influx of expats from South and North America has locals calling the city the “Miami of Europe.” But don’t let that dissuade you. Mallorquín designer Rosa Esteva, who designs the elegant, made-in-Spain fashion brand Cortana, emphasizes “the charm of those glorious old places that have survived through time.” That means staying at hotels like the intimate Hotel Orfila, booking a table at La Parra, wandering through El Rastro, Madrid’s legendary flea market, and checking out a late-night flamenco show at Tablao de la Villa. At the same time, contemporary places like Esteva’s new shop in the Salamanca neighborhood, the modern tapas bar Sala de Despiece, and the contemporary-art gallery Albarrán Bourdais are worth checking out.

The typical Spanish itinerary often includes a few days in Barcelona to take in the Gaudí before heading south to the beaches of Andalusia. But Vella González, the founder of fashion brand Boxcalf, which has a flagship in Madrid’s Malasaña neighborhood, extols northern Spain’s charms and cooler climate. “For non-Spaniards, it’s an undiscovered paradise,” she says. Start in San Sebastián, one of the world’s most celebrated gastronomic capitals, and eat your way through its pintxos bars, finishing with a steak at the Basque grill house Portuetxe.

In Bilbao, discover the next generation of art spaces, such as the light-filled expansion of the Bilbao Fine Arts Museum, designed by Norman Foster and Luis María Uriarte. The Bilbao effect can be felt in nearby Santander, thanks to the new Faro Santander museum and cultural space, a historic building reimagined by David Chipperfield and currently showcasing the works of surrealist painter Leonora Carrington. Move on to the pristine beaches, green hills, and exceptional dining scene of the Asturias and Galicia regions. In Asturias, splurge on a stay at the remote wabi-sabi styled Solo Palacio and explore the old-growth forests and prehistoric rock shelters of Las Ubiñas-La Mesa Natural Park. Cozy up in the Casa Beatnik Country House hotel in Galicia, and walk the last 10 miles of the famed Camino de Santiago trail to Santiago de Compostela and its Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage site. It’s an idyllic ending to a new kind of Spanish pilgrimage.

#6749. Margot Robbie’s Side-Parted ‘Buttercup Bob’ Is Polished and Easy to Wear: How to Try It Now

The actor and producer proves how a simple styling switch can make all the difference.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There are few hair updates as simple, yet as impactful, as switching up your part. After several seasons dominated by center-parted lengths and deliberately undone styling, the side part is making a convincing return. The latest to make a case for its appeal? None other than Margot Robbie.

Attending Chanel’s Cruise 2026/2027 show in Australia, the actor and producer stepped out with a softly structured ‘buttercup bob,’ styled with a deep side part and flipped-out ends. The result was equal parts polished and quietly sophisticated. And while Robbie has recently been favoring the waterfall bob, this latest iteration feels notably sleeker, offering a more refined take on the trending cut.

“This bob is an effortless take on a classic jaw-length cut. It’s neat without feeling rigid, with soft ends and a clean shape that gives hair an expensive-looking finish,” Luke Hersheson, hairstylist and CEO of Hershesons previously told ELLE. In short, it trades lived-in texture for a more polished silhouette, with precise ends and subtle flicks upward that create a sharper finish.

Robbie’s latest style embodies the look perfectly, pairing a side part with softly sculpted ends for an updated take on the preppy bob. The part allows for a sweeping side bang, adding a touch of glamour to an otherwise classic cut.

When it comes to re-creating Robbie’s look, Talia Hurley, a stylist at Blue Tit London, recommends blow-drying the hair with a round brush for a glossy, classic finish. This will also help create added volume and the bend needed to achieve the look’s side-swept shape.

Luke Hersheson recommends finishing the look with a pea-sized amount of smoothing cream to add shine and tame flyaways without leaving the hair greasy, ensuring the style retains its polished, glossy finish.

#6744. All the Gifts GQ Editors Want This Holiday Season 2026

As the desk at GQ that handles all things shopping, the GQ Recommends team has developed a rather motley assortment of wants, needs, and highly specific desires. We have good taste, if I may say as much, and no shortage of opinions about what makes a thing worth owning. So this holiday season, I asked everyone to set aside the usual assignments and show me what's on their own wishlists. What follows is an eclectic grab bag of A1 gifts, straight from the folks who spend all year finding the good stuff.

Still got names to cross off? Peruse our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more good stuff worth giving (or keeping).

Years after getting married, I can say with confidence that the best thing about marriage is my wife. But a close second is the set of Sabre Bistrot flatware we received off our registry. A pleasure to hold and behold. And now they make chopsticks, which is unfortunate news for someone afflicted with my particular strain of completism. I have no choice but to finish the set. —MN

I couldn’t in good conscience ask for everything I want from Camiel Fortgens, which is, uh, everything. But this heavy-knit beanie, with the melange yarn and signature raw edges, feels like a reasonable place to start. —MN

It's true, the best radio station on the internet deserves its own hardware. Made in collaboration with tech company Atonemo, this dedicated player has big, tactile buttons for tuning into NTS 1 and 2, a dial for wandering through the Infinite Mixtapes, and the ability to plug straight into my amp. I feel so alive, and I've never been more excited to turn a dial. —MN

Nosying around other people’s bookshelves is a favorite pastime, and I can think of only a few libraries I’d rather rifle through than Luis Barragan’s. I’ve made the pilgrimage to his home and studio in Mexico City, and this new book offers a new look at the peerless architect’s life and influences through the personal collection he kept on his shelves. —MN

You may already know that we love Lady White’s top-tier white T-shirts, but we’re also massive fans of their sweats, especially this superweight hoodie. And when they say superweight, they mean it. I’ve own the zip-up version, and it's basically a winter coat. This will become my dog-walking hoodie, my 6 A.M. stroll to the bodega hoodie, and the late-night walk back from the cinema hoodie. —JB

Back in high school, some homies and I thought of ourselves as future producers. The music was terrible and thankfully is lost in the ether somewhere on SoundCloud, but despite those early attempts, I still find sampling a fascinating part of music. It’s a way to shut off the brain and think about songs in a new way. I doubt the music will be any better than it was back in the day, but I’ll have fun acting like Jamie XX or Nicolas Jaar, at least. —JB

I’m a pen-and-paper guy. You will often catch me feverishly jotting down thoughts in the middle of a meeting. I’ve recently needed to retire my old Moleskine notebook and found myself doing a deep dive into reusable leather-bound book holders that you can treat like a modular journal. You can add in different types of notebooks, calendars, and daily planners—the possibilities are endless. —JB

There comes a time in every man's life when he fancies himself a barista and thinks he should dedicate some time to learning how to pull a damn good espresso. I am that man, and the delusions are more errant than you would expect. Because I drink so much coffee, I’ve convinced myself I might as well get good at making it. —JB

As much as I don’t want to admit that I overindex on outerwear, my closet tells the truth. It’s so full that I can’t even shift any of the hangers without taking one of them out first. But that won’t stop me from eyeing this gorgeous coat from Auralee. It’s everything I want in a coat: dramatically long, artfully faded, and a deep black colorway. Now I’ll just have to find a new coat rack. —GO

I saw this bad boy in a shop and was so drawn to it. The colors are just right, the size is great, and the material is ultra-sturdy, but on this day, the devil on my shoulder told me not to get it that day. I came to my senses and came back the next day only to find that the tote was sold out. Hence why I’ve got it on my wish list because I believe in second chances and miracles. —GO

This little thing is a clever ear warmer that can be worn as is or can be slipped over the bill of your favorite hat. It’s silly and weird and cool and totally unnecessary. And yet, I would not be mad if this made its way into my stocking. —GO

I’ve always wanted a true Neapolitan-style jacket and getting to try on some of Natalino’s pieces in person during a pop-up in NYC has only stoked the fire. From the hand-stitched entails to the soft shoulders to the absolutely supreme fit, there’s no better jacket in my mind. —GO

No, I am not a ne'er-do-well Italian playboy loath to step into a leadership position at my dad's sprawling imports company. Yes, I would like to dress like one. —AG

Leave it to the vintage fiends in Japan to turn up a version of JCPenney’s canonical Big Mac flannel—the greatest flannel ever made, FYI—that might actually be worth the asking price. —AG

Okay, okay, okay. Once the sticker shock has worn off, think about how good of a boy I’ve been this year… —AG

You could drop $100K on leg-lengthening surgery and then rebuild your jeans rotation from scratch. Or you could just buy La Botte Gardiane’s naturally height-enhancing boots, which look great with the jeans you already own. —AG

I used to question whether the Eadem hype was another fad born of bloated influencer budgets, but dude. This balm is legit. I want every single color. You should get this for your girl for the holidays. If you’re scared of picking colors for her, opt for “Butter Mochi” (clear! unscented!) or “Sakura Shaved Ice,” a light pink that complements nearly every lip combo under the sun. —MH

I was treating my guy to his first ever foray into Buck Mason when I clocked a store employee wearing the Roper Jean and immediately lost the plot RE: which T-shirt the boy was trying on next. The silhouette! The wash! The contrast stitching! The complimentary Buck Mason tailoring for my stubby little legs! A girl can dream. A girl is still dreaming. Someone please gift this to me. —MH

Confessions of an adult seasonal allergies sufferer: I open the windows to air out my apartment despite knowing that that’s just welcoming the allergens into my home. Practical people might say I should address the issue at the root, but where’s the whimsy in that? Wouldn’t capitalism prefer that I purchase a solution to my problem instead? —MH

It took only one year at GQ and one “welcome to the team” bottle of D.S.&Durga to turn me into a fragrance fiend. For my bank account’s sake, I made a No New Fragrances vow earlier this summer … but gifts don’t count as breaking that pledge. Also, I really need a winter scent; my beloved Eau Splendide is more of a summer gal. —MH

I already own a bottle of Naked Dance, and it’s dangerously close to empty, which is the highest compliment I can give a fragrance. Well, the second highest. The first is how often I’m asked what fragrance I’m wearing, and I’m not ready to give that up. It’s a cult pick from a tiny niche house, right down to the cap, which is handmade from wood scraps and resin, exactly the kind of detail I can’t resist. —AH

I’m a vintage obsessive at heart, and this bracelet has that worn-in, one-of-a-kind look I’m always drawn to. Pyrite is also known as fool’s gold, and frankly, I’d be a fool not to want it. —AH

A good belt is the most underrated piece in any outfit, and my studded belt collection could always use one more. I’ve reached the point where I pick my outfits around my belts, not the other way around, and this one already has a few looks planned. The most practical gift on my list? I think so. —AH

All fall I’ve been hunting for the perfect pair of cords, mostly because I’m notorious for wearing the same pants almost every day. These feel like they walked straight out of a ’70s record sleeve, with that soft, slouchy fit. They’d slot into my current wardrobe perfectly, and finally give my usual pair a break. —AH

I love a gift you can give and secretly steal for yourself. This bathrobe is a “thoughtfu” gift for your partner that you’ll get to commandeer when they’re not looking. Two for the price of one really. You’re welcome! —LP

It’s a cliché, but the best gifts are the ones you wouldn’t buy for yourself but desperately want. And who doesn’t want a chic, soft, luxurious, well-designed towel? No one, is the answer. Tekla has a knack for unexpected color combinations that should feel wrong but somehow feel so right (this pink and brown combo is excellent)—a mood booster for any bathroom. Oh, and they’re unisex, making them a handy option when you have a last-minute gift to give. —LP

There is a myth that shower gel, or “smellies” as we call them in the UK (I’m British), are thoughtless gifts. I disagree. A luxury shower gel will add a little something extra to your morning routine, or someone else’s, and is a crowd pleaser for secret santa. This specific wash I can attest also smells incredible. —LP

Last holiday season, I treated my mother to a pair of Jenni Kayne cashmere socks. Since then, she’s never looked back and now has an expectation that Christmas = cashmere. She deserves it, so I’m happy to oblige (I may as well buy myself a pair at the checkout whilst I’m at it). They make a great gift for anyone who loves a cozy weekend at home or wants something luxurious to slip into after a day of hiking or skiing (my personal favourite time to treat my feet). —LP

A couple of decades ago, Helmut Lang was the place to go for a more city-minded denim jacket. And while those pieces still do numbers on the second-hand market, I’ve always found them a touch too fitted. So imagine my relief to discover this roomier Kaptain Sunshine take, which still feels special (and office-appropriate) due to its pleats, dark color, and smart single pocket. —LC

As a teenager, I was completely taken by this scent. Then, throughout my twenties, I tried all of the nicher body washes I thought I was meant to like. The ones that smelled like herb gardens, cedar forests, or sometimes… nothing at all. But following a recent, delayed flight-induced spin around Duty Free, I was reunited with Re-Charge Black Pepper. Please, kind gifters, reunite me with even more of it. —LC

Not just a stunning book about jazz and America in the 1960s, but also hundreds of pages of incredible style. I’m hoping to deepen my understanding of the music over the holidays, and know it would only help to be leafing through this as I do so. —LC

As with the Molton Brown above, I’m done surveying the market: I feel my best in these! And I’d wager the men (and women) in your life likely do too. —LC

Genetics haven’t exactly done some of us any favors in the under-eye department (me, I'm talking about me), but this eye cream levels the playing field. It works beautifully for me, and it’s exactly the kind of splurge that makes a great gift. —EH

Experiment is one of the most exciting skincare brands I’ve come across lately, with a thoughtfully edited lineup that doesn’t try to do too much. Its new mini set is a great introduction, featuring what I think is an underrated ingredient: glycerin. It helps skin hold onto moisture, which is exactly what my thirsty skin craves in these drier times. —EH

Vitaly has been on my radar for years, and I’ve had my eye on more than few of its chains and rings. It just launched an Art Deco line, which is a glorious mix of classic style and signature industrial Vitaly edge. While a lot of the larger statement pieces are on my wishlist, the Tier Chain feels like a daily driver and a statement piece at the same time. —EH

Once we get through the joyfully chaotic holidays, the new year calls for rest and relaxation. While cozy socks and a soft throw are always welcome gifts, this blanket feels like an ultimate upgrade. Weighted for gentle relaxing pressure and heated for warmth even in the chilliest rooms. Sounds like a recipe for the sweetest of dreams! —EH

#6743. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6740. RIP to LIV, the Golf League No One Ever Really Cared About

The most remarkable thing about the era of LIV Golf, a five-year run characterized by near-parodic blunders and missteps, is that leadership and its public-facing talent don’t appear to have learned any lessons from their many failures.

From the beginning, the upstart league, established in 2021 as a rival to the dominant PGA Tour, was plagued by its own ineptitude. It’s only fitting—after LIV’s newfound lifeline, private investment firm BC Partners, reneged on a $300 million investment—that the brand’s figureheads are now celebrating the end by taking a victory lap. Tone-deaf doesn’t begin to describe it.

LIV CEO Scott O’Neil—who took over for original boss and Major winner Greg Norman in January of 2025 and was faced with finding new cash flow after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it would no longer finance the operation—clearly exists in a different reality than our own. “Together, our team delivered world-class individual and team competitions across five continents, built a global business, secured pathways to The Open and U.S. Open… and built a league capable of attracting both elite and rising talent from around the world,” he said in a statement late last week. It’s unclear if the farewell tour will continue, though, an even newer report suggests that BC is looking to purchase a bankruptcy loan from LIV’s current owners. If this Hail Mary works, LIV’s future would look much different than the one O’Neil has promised.

Another way to look at it? One of LIV’s biggest accomplishments was that the league, despite its intentions to diversify the game and bring fun back into a sport that had come to personify privilege and exclusivity, inadvertently consolidated the PGA Tour’s power as a monopolistic behemoth now primed to solidify its status as the only league in town. They helped usher in a new era of leadership and investment for the Tour, including the introduction of CEO Brian Rolapp, who is by all accounts the most well-liked and accomplished boss it’s had in quite some time.

LIV also managed to tarnish the reputations of its biggest stars. Jon Rahm, who was vehemently opposed to the dog and pony show when it was announced, only to sheepishly take a bag of blood money so big his great grandchildren will never have to work a day in their lives, is now one of the game’s great “What If?” stories. Prior to the US Open at Brookline Country Club in June 2022, the defending champion was asked about his thoughts on the upstart league. “Money is great,” he said. But Rahm and his wife thought about it further. “Will our lifestyle change if I got $400 million? No, it will not change one bit.” Just over a year later, he defected to LIV.

Then there’s Phil Mickelson, who was poised to become a fixture of the American Ryder Cup team and widely considered a shoo-in to hold a cushy job as an analyst for golf’s biggest broadcasting events. Upon joining the league, he admitted in a conversation with Alan Shipnuck that Saudi Arabia was a terrible bedfellow. (Shipnuck and Mickelson have disagreed over whether the comments were on or off the record.) “They killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights. They execute people over there for being gay,” he explained. But there was a caveat: LIV was simply a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to reshape how the PGA Tour operates.” Miraculously, he got that part right.

Prize money on the PGA Tour is greater than ever, the Tour’s main events have recalibrated, and its season-ending championship series has been completely reimagined. Mickelson won’t be allowed within 100 miles of it.

The league’s biggest attraction, Bryson DeChambeau, is theoretically the worst-situated of the game’s many turncoats, though he’s probably more excited about growing his YouTube channel than he is about playing golf anyway. No one’s put their reputation on the line for this gaggle of buffoons quite like DeChambeau, who spoke proudly about how LIV was “growing the game” and “bringing team golf to the world.” This past weekend, he shared a statement on the dissolution of LIV. “I still believe in team golf,” he wrote. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.” A loyal foot soldier, even from the grave.

It was always about the money. Nothing more, nothing less. This was a cash grab of epic proportions, and golfers not good enough to earn their keep on the PGA Tour took a life raft and briefly found themselves in possession of luxury superyachts. Then, low tide left them holding bags of cash and not much else. Was it worth it? For most of these golfers, probably. They were past their primes when LIV began; they’re still past the primes now, and just a helluva lot richer.

The league positioned itself as a disruptor, and disrupted so poorly that they’ve turned the PGA Tour into the strongest version of itself we’ve seen since Tiger Woods was at his peak. All that bloviating about the good of LIV Golf from its loudest talking heads is a bunch of nonsense.

It’s hard to tell if these statements are one last line of defense or more genuine delusion from LIV’s last advocates. They came in with the idea of sticking it to the PGA Tour, which at the time was facing bleak circumstances, bogged down in nonsense before redirecting its energy towards batting this gnat into extinction. Ultimately, LIV helped the PGA Tour save itself.

Now it’s gone for good, and five billion dollars later, we’re not gonna remember a damn thing about it. Not the players, not the leadership, and surely not all the ways they supposedly grew the game while merely growing their own bank accounts.

#6738. The Best Conditioners for Fine Hair for Lightweight Hydration and Repair

If you have fine hair, you probably have a conditioner routine that looks a lot like mine: a tiny amount, only on the very ends, rinsed out almost immediately, just in case. For years, I was so afraid of flat roots that I barely conditioned at all, and my ends showed it. They tangled, frizzed and snapped every time I brushed them, and my bangs never quite sat right. On the days I did use a proper amount, I’d end up washing my hair again the next morning because it already looked greasy.

Eventually, I figured out the amount wasn’t the issue. I’d just been using the wrong conditioners. Fine hair has narrow strands, so the rich formulas made for thick, dry hair don’t really sink in. They sit on top and drag everything down. What works better is something light that rinses out clean and still leaves your hair soft enough to brush through. A few also have powerful ingredients like rice protein, biotin, or panthenol, which make each strand feel a bit thicker and look fuller. How you use it matters, too. Keeping most of it on your mid-lengths and ends, and rinsing well at the scalp, makes a bigger difference than you’d expect.

Once you’ve got both the formula and the technique right, second-day hair gets a lot easier to deal with. Below, the best conditioners for fine hair, according to celebrity hairstylists and Vogue editors.

Should I use conditioner for thin, fine hair?

Yes you should use conditioner for fine hair. Skipping conditioner might keep your roots from falling flat, but your ends will end up tangled, frizzy and more likely to break. Just pick a light formula, and don’t expect it to change how much hair you have, even if the bottle says “thickening.” “You’re not actually changing the natural thickness of the hair or stimulating new growth,” says Cook. “You’re creating the look and feel of denser, fuller hair. I love this approach, especially for fine hair that needs body without sacrificing movement or softness.” Kreager is less convinced by thickening formulas, which she says mostly “over cleanse or coat the hair strand,” so she sticks with a lightweight conditioner that keeps hair soft without weighing it down.

How should I apply conditioner if I have fine hair?

Start with less than you think you need and keep most of it on your mid-lengths and ends, unless you’re using a formula made for the scalp, like Medicube’s. Macias also uses this step to detangle. “I start from the ends and gradually work upward, rather than pulling a brush directly through from the roots,” he says. Rinsing matters just as much as applying, especially near the scalp. “One of the biggest mistakes people make with conditioning products is assuming that leaving a little extra behind will provide more hydration,” he says. “In reality, residual from products can sometimes make the roots appear flatter and affect how the hair responds to styling.”

#6736. Nicole Kidman’s Long ‘Almond Cream’ Nails Are the Sophisticated Go-With-Everything Trend to Try Now: Get the Look

This manicure proves long almond nails never go out of style.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There are certain manicures that never go out of style, regardless of the season. Case in point: Nicole Kidman’s long ‘almond cream’ nails. Spotted at the LACMA Art+Film Gala wearing softly tapered almond nails in a glossy milky shade, the actor’s manicure served as a reminder that winter manicures needn’t be dark or glittery to make an impact.

“Kidman’s nails are a great example of how to wear a longer length without them looking too dramatic,” says Susan Carroll, founder of Young LDN. “The almond shape is one of my favorites because it’s incredibly flattering on the hands. The sides taper in slightly before finishing in a soft, rounded point, which helps elongate the fingers and gives a much more delicate appearance than a square or coffin shape.”

Serving as an ideal entry point for anyone looking to experiment with longer nails without committing to a dramatic stiletto shape, the almond silhouette offers a more wearable alternative. Carroll also recommends adapting the length to suit your lifestyle and comfort level. The appeal lies in its versatility, as it can be easily achieved without the need for extensions. “The shape does a lot of the work, and keeping the color subtle makes the overall look feel much more elegant,” she adds.

Re-creating the look is very straightforward, as the key lies in the shape. Ask your nail technician for a soft almond silhouette with rounded tips, rather than anything too sharply pointed. “The key is making sure the nails are evenly shaped and the cuticles are tidy, as there’s nowhere to hide imperfections with such a simple manicure,” says Carroll. To finish, simply apply two coats of a sheer milky beige polish before sealing with a glossy top coat for a light-reflecting finish.

The result is an effortlessly elegant manicure that feels equal parts timeless and wearable.

#6735. How Martine Rose Became Menswear’s Secret Weapon

After much speculation, the fashion rumors were true: Martine Rose is officially Balenciaga’s next creative director. It’s undoubtedly her biggest job yet—and a historic appointment: she is the first woman creative director to lead the French house. Rose succeeds Valentino vet Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure after just three seasons was announced yesterday. This is a major moment for the British-Jamaican designer, who has spent nearly two decades building a namesake label that wields outsize influence.

Rose has long occupied a curious position in menswear: a designer’s designer with a devoted following of both high-fashion heads and the streetwear obsessed. Since launching her eponymous brand in 2007, she’s developed an unmistakable visual language of playful styling, graphic-driven sportswear, offbeat tailoring, and covetable sneaker collabs. Her clothes take the familiar and make it strange, infusing everyday garments with humor, a touch of romance, and occasionally an ugly-chic sensibility: think square-toed loafers, chap-covered suit trousers, and soccer jerseys with lace-up fastenings. The results can be loud, wildly stylish, and routinely fun.

“I’ve always been drawn to the way men are told to dress,” the designer told GQ in 2023. She’s been on a mission to subvert those conventions ever since.

On the Martine Rose runway, sportswear and tailoring regularly share the spotlight. Much of that sensibility comes from her ability to borrow from and fuse London’s historic subcultures: ravers and club kids, football fanatics and nattily dressed mods. She tends to embrace the unusual and eccentric rather than focusing on making everything read as conventionally stylish. One look from a recent collection featured a swishy track jacket tucked into straight-leg blue jeans, and another paired a perfectly tailored coat with athletic shorts and knee-high socks. In Rose’s universe, there is no wrong way to mix and match. That’s part of her charm.

That sensibility eventually caught the eye of Demna during his decade-long tenure as Balenciaga’s creative director. The firebrand Georgian designer reached out to Rose in 2015, and she spent the next three years as a menswear consultant for the house during a high-profile era defined by supersized proportions and outlandish accessories. The blazers were big and the boots were bigger, but the star power of the celebrities who wore them was the biggest of all.

Rose is no stranger to dressing famous people. Her clothes have landed on some of the most photographed men in the world: Drake, Timothée Chalamet, Bad Bunny, A$AP Rocky. Perhaps her most visible endorsement came at the 2025 Super Bowl, when Kendrick Lamar strutted around the halftime show in a custom red, white, and blue leather varsity jacket designed by Rose. (In 2023, the rapper had boasted about how he wears “Martine when I board jets” on the Baby Keem track “The Hillbillies”; a year later, he sported several of her designs in his “Not Like Us” video.) Over the years, Rose has become one of the rare designers whose collections are covered by both Vogue and Hypebeast, a testament to her appeal across fashion’s various tribes. She’s been a fixture at London Fashion Week, and made her Milan debut in 2024. She has two hit Supreme collaborations under her belt. When Nike came calling, Rose produced remixed versions of the Shox (which Lamar wore while he accepted three Grammys in 2023) and Monarch sneakers—turning two of the Swoosh’s most divisive silhouettes into lustworthy objects. Tommy Hilfiger enlisted her for a collection centered on the streetwise style of Tommy Jeans in the ’90s. Brands know she can deliver the goods.

Which brings us back to the Balenciaga appointment. Rose obviously knows the house, or at least Demna’s vision for it—a vision that brought meme-worthy fashion but also massive creative and commercial success. A statement from Luca de Meo, CEO of Kering (the French luxury group that owns Balenciaga), included all the boilerplate press language about innovation, creativity, and culture. More crucially, Rose has proven she can make familiar clothes feel fresh, taking what guys are already wearing and turning them into something surprising and covetable. The question is now what Rose will be able to do with the resources of a global luxury powerhouse at her disposal. She’s spent much of her career building her own idiosyncratic world at Martine Rose. At Balenciaga, she’ll find herself on a much bigger stage with a vast audience and a completely new rulebook.

In 2020, when discussing her reputation as something of an underground darling, Rose told GQ: “I’ve never really wanted to be part of a big thing. Anything that is mainstream—since I was small—hasn’t really appealed to me.” Six years later, she’s earned one of the biggest jobs in fashion. There’s great fun in evolution, too.

#6733. You’re Going to Want to Keep an Eye on Eldar Isgandarov

Last month, Eldar Isgandarov attended Julio Torres’s Halloween party dressed as Candace, co-owner of the radical feminist bookstore Women & Women First on the sketch comedy series Portlandia. This was an important place to begin our conversation: Isgandarov wanted to explain why his halo of brown curls was a bit mussed. The night prior, he’d donned a wig cap and a long blond wig. He tried to stick close to his friend—who went as Candace’s partner, Toni—throughout the night. “If you separate, it gets tricky,” he says. Otherwise, “they’d think she’s Velma and I’m Lucius Malfoy.”

Isgandarov, an Azerbaijani actor who lives in Bushwick with roommates and a cat named Cheese, has charmed audiences this fall in his role as Nicky, a self-described “aspiring queer philosopher,” in Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut, Club Kid. Calling Nicky the roommate of Firstman’s Peter would somewhat overstate their arrangement: He’s a video game-addicted layabout crashing in Peter’s rent-controlled loft. When Peter finally kicks him out to make room for Arlo (Reggie Absolom), the 10-year-old son he didn’t realize he had, Nicky moves in with their eccentric downstairs neighbor, Evelyn (Colleen Camp). The two soon become an irresistibly silly comic duo.

Isgandarov admits to being nervous about doing the film at first; he wasn’t sure how its overt gayness would be received back home. But an early meeting with Firstman assured him that he was in capable hands. “My first little rendezvous with Jordan before we started filming, I was like, ‘Oh, this guy is a maestro.’”

He credits the easy, funny chemistry between Nicky and Evelyn to both the atmosphere on set—Firstman encouraged his cast to try things out—and to Camp, whom Isgandarov calls a “generous actor.” “People keep saying we should do a spinoff,” he says, “and I would love to do it, but I would get tired of laughing. We would constantly be breaking. That would be the hardest thing to do.” Their storyline also suited him as someone who is “good with moms” and grew up obsessed with Sunset Boulevard’s Norma Desmond. “I was like, oh my God, I’m in love with this woman. Like, I wanna marry her, and I wanna be with her forever, no matter how fucked-up she is,” he remembers with a laugh.

In December, Isgandarov will appear in Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut, the story of a woman whose life is transformed when she’s cast in her community theater’s latest production. “They are your mentors, but they’re also not,” he says of working with stars Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti. “Like, they’re your best friends on set.”

His first day shooting was also his first day ever on a professional set; until then, he’d only done student films during his time at Savannah College of Art and Design. His first scene set him opposite Giamatti, with many other actors looking on. After a pep talk from fellow castmate Havana Rose Liu, Isgandarov was off. “It was intoxicatingly fun,” he says. “It was like Disneyland, you know? As a kid you go and you’re like, ‘Oh my God! Magic is real.’”

As a former theater kid, he also thrilled at the chance to work on a film about musical theater. He identifies as a Sondheim fanatic, referring to Sunday in the Park with George and Passion as two of his favorite shows. (As it happens, none but Sondheim muse Bernadette Peters, who originated the role of Dot in Sunday, makes a cameo in The Debut, though she and Isgandarov had no scenes together.) He recalls sitting out a visit to Basement—the notorious, semi-exclusive nightclub in Queens—with his friends in order to watch a proshot at home. “And the good thing about the fact that I didn’t go is that they got rejected at the door,” he deadpans.

Indeed, despite his breakout role in Club Kid, Isgandarov likes to keep a low profile. “I like hanging out. I like a good, real conversation. Not that you can’t have that when you’re partying, but a club can be very overwhelming at times.” Sometimes even a club kid needs a night in.

#6732. 50 Marathons in 24 Days. Men Are Inventing Extreme Physical Challenges for the Hell of It

For more than 18 days straight this past May, Mason Wright woke up every morning at 5 a.m. and ran laps around a track at a high school in Layton, Utah. The early-spring air was typically crisp, and the smell of dew-covered grass reminded him of childhood. By the time students would arrive for class, he’d have run 10 miles. At lunch, he kept running. And when student athletes came out for after-school track practice he would still be there, running alongside them. When the sun finally set over the mountains, he’d crawl into a van parked beside the field, sleep as much as he could, and do it all over again. He ran through freezing mornings that left frost on the ground and rainstorms that flooded the track, leaving his feet so waterlogged that his skin split open.

When Wright finished his extended sprint, he became the third person in the world to run 1,000 fairly consecutive miles around a track, a project he embarked upon because, as he puts it, “I wanted something that genuinely sounded impossible.”

Mason Wright camped nearby a high school track to complete a self-assigned challenge of running 1,000 consecutive miles in a row.

When Wright finished his extended sprint, he became the third person in the world to run 1,000 fairly consecutive miles around a track.

“I wanted something that genuinely sounded impossible,” Wright says of the project.

Wright isn’t the only one with an appetite for the absurd. There’s now a never-ending slew of guys inventing and completing preposterous physical challenges, often with elaborate, self-imposed rules meant to make them as miserable as humanly possible. Many have teams chronicling every grueling mile and setback online. If they manage to pull it off the challenge, they emerge as semi-viral niche sports heroes in their corner of the fitness internet. In 2020, ultramarathoner and Navy Seal David Goggins launched his annual 4x4x48 challenge, inviting his followers to run four miles every four hours for 48 hours. In December 2025, UK-based athlete Travis Kerry set the world record for longest nonstop bear crawl after bear crawling 50 kilometers (31 miles) across the streets of London, and nine months later Kevin Ocipeka from Germany burpee broad-jumped his way 26.2 miles along a track in 155 hours, 44 minutes, and 51 seconds—longer and faster than anyone had burpeed before.

“There’s this flywheel effect of extreme one-upmanship going on on social media,” says Michael Ceely, a psychotherapist and high-performance coach who works with athletes.

But beyond bragging rights, why are men motivated to push themselves to such dire limits? And what, exactly, are they getting out of it?

Many of the men I spoke to for this piece are drawn to the unknown. Once they have an idea, they hyperfixate on it until they accomplish it. Professional mountain biker Matt Jones says the concepts come from just about anywhere. “That’s how my brain works,” he says. He can’t drive past a rooftop or construction crane without wondering whether he could ride it or jump off it. “It doesn’t take long before you start going down a rabbit hole of crazy ideas, and then actually becoming obsessed with them enough to wanna do them,” he says. For the stunt he pulled off in November 2025, he spent months calculating the precise timing needed to jump through the open trailers of two trucks traveling in opposite directions, with only a split-second margin for error.

Matt Jones in Sweden strategizing for his 2025 ‘Through’ project, in which he jumped through the open trailers of two trucks traveling in opposite directions.

Matt Jones performed a world first jumping between two moving trucks.

William Goodge, an ultrarunner who embarked on the arduous task of running 50 marathons in 50 states in 24 days this October, is similarly attracted to the uncertainty that comes with each challenge. “If I wasn’t scared by it, I wouldn’t be enthusiastic,” he says. “That’s the whole point in this journey for me.” His quest, which culminated at this year’s NYC marathon, was nearly as logistically challenging as it was physically demanding. A flight delay or bad weather could have set him back a few hours, potentially derailing his entire schedule. On four of the days, he needed to run three marathons with only short stretches of rest or travel between them.

The thrill of chasing a near-impossible goal can seem grim once you’re in the thick of it, though, and that misery is equally part of the appeal. Kerry had dreamed of earning a Guinness World Record since childhood, and when he saw someone bear-crawl a marathon, he decided to take the record even further: 31 miles, compared to 26. He tested the movement on a treadmill, taking 20 minutes to cover a single kilometer. It was, he says, “the hardest fucking thing I’ve ever done.” But he figured if he could do one kilometer, he could do 50. “It’s just one 50 times, and I just need to get better at it,” he says.

Yet halfway through his bear crawl across the cobbled streets of London, rain was coming down, his hands were cold, and he was wearing a pair of garden gloves he had cut the fingertips off to prevent his palms from getting torn on the pavement. “One of my best mate’s jobs the whole time was squeezing water like a literal udder out the end of my gloves,” he says. Kerry thought about calling it quits. “Even though I physically wasn’t at the end of my limit, mentally I was like, I just can’t do this anymore,” he says.

UK-based athlete Travis Kerry completed a 50-kilometer bear crawl across the cobbled streets of London in 2025.

Kerry still hasn't regained feeling in his fingertips after completing the challenge. “I don’t know if that’s ever gonna come back,” he says. “A small price to pay.”

His coach could tell he was losing steam, so she told him to stand up and scream. “I went to the edge of Tower Bridge and screamed the word ‘fuck’ as loud as I possibly could,” he says. The release felt incredible. He got back down on his hands and feet and kept crawling.

Despite the sense of accomplishment they represent, these feats can come at a serious physical cost. Both Wright and Kerry say they may have suffered permanent nerve damage after their massive efforts. Wright, who ran 400 miles on stress fractures, says the pain that would take over his body was “unbearable.” Kerry hasn’t regained feeling in his fingertips. “I don’t know if that’s ever gonna come back,” he says. “A small price to pay.” Jones acknowledges that he’s spent most of his most epic moments in the last 10 years in physical pain. “I think there’s a limit to the force you can take and the number of years you can take it for,” he says.

The men who do these challenges put their bodies through hell in the search for personal growth and self-discovery. Take Goodge. He began running after losing his mom to cancer. “I wanted to feel physical pain to deal with the mental and spiritual pain of what I was going through,” he says. Compared with what she endured, he says, his own discomfort seems trivial. “I’m doing it in her honor. I’m doing it for Stand Up to Cancer. I can carry on. I’ve got no excuse not to take another step.”

Wright also found himself confronting the grief of losing his father when he was younger during his 1,000-mile run. “When you lose someone close to you, your world stops, but the world around you continues,” he says. “You almost feel like you’re stuck in time.” Running endless laps around the same track while the students’ lives continued brought that feeling back. “It forces you to let go of these things or else you’ll go more crazy,” he says.

Matt Valaoras, who holds hours-long planks at music festivals and sporting events, started planking as a way to manage his anxiety. As a college student, he could only plank for 45 seconds, but he added on time every day until he could hold it for several hours. As he’s held his core steady through rough conditions (the worst of which was a swarm of bugs biting him while he planked the duration of a Savannah Bananas baseball game), he’s “stacked the evidence” that he can handle anything that’s thrown at him—physical or otherwise. “I can confidently say, ‘Okay, I can do this because I, I did that, and it was worse than I expected,’” he says.

Ceely says it’s common that physical suffering can sometimes be a socially acceptable way for men to process emotional suffering. “Men have a hard time expressing weakness or vulnerability or saying ‘I just feel bad, period,’” he says. “They want to say, ‘Here’s what I did to fix it.’ Which, in a way, is a healthy coping mechanism. It’s better than being depressed.”

Valaoras acknowledges that this is part of the equation for him. “For a lot of guys, myself included, it’s easier to exhaust yourself physically than explain what’s exhausting you mentally. I’ve definitely used exercise as a way to avoid confronting things emotionally.” Nevertheless, he says that following some kind of physical exertion, he feels more comfortable opening up.

Meanwhile, Kerry says that he uses his emotional suffering as a way of fueling his physical feats. “One who chooses suffering is choosing to use their brain’s deflection mechanism to channel that emotional suffering into physical capabilities,” he says. He references the so-called pain cave—a term that many distance runners have used to describe the most miserable moments of an event, when the brain and body start to wear thin. “By focusing on that emotional trigger,” he says, that “becomes the person’s ‘why’.”

This form of emotional release can create a powerful cycle of anticipation and reward—encouraging more and more challenges. “You get adrenaline, endorphins, dopamine,” Ceely says. “There’s a physiological kind of addiction that can start just because you’re human and you’re wired that way.”

And it becomes a lot harder to stop if you have an audience expecting an encore. While most of the athletes I spoke to insisted they would still be doing these challenges if no one was watching, social media introduces pressure and expectations; it “moves the goalposts because the wilder the idea is, the more it sets the standards and moves the bar,” says Jones. Wright acknowledges that you can’t “run these miles and post about it on social media without some ego involved.” As he planned his track run, he was set on doubling the stakes of his last challenge, which was a 421-mile run across Utah. “800 miles isn’t cool, so it had to be 1,000,” he says.

Jones says he wouldn’t attempt his most outlandish stunts without the pressure to hold onto his brand sponsorships or please the fans in his comment sections. He, unlike most men who we spoke to for this piece, is a professional Red Bull athlete, whose livelihood in part depends on pulling off these spectacles. “Would I jump through two moving trucks just for a laugh? Probably not,” he says. “No, I wouldn’t at all.” He nevertheless enjoys his audience’s admiration. “I guess that’s vanity in a way, isn’t it?” he says. “But it’s also the currency of what we do.”

None of these men seem particularly interested in finding a comfortable stopping point. Wright says he has yet to find his limit. Valaoras has world records attempts in mind. Goodge doesn’t plan on slowing down.

“I want to be on the edge. How close can we get without falling off?” Goodge says. “How close to the sun can we fly, like Icarus, and not get burnt?”

#6729. Jolie Made the Showerhead a Beauty Staple. What’s Next?

A showerhead is not an obvious candidate for brand cachet. Yet Jolie has turned one of the bathroom’s most overlooked fixtures into a beauty-wellness product and a conversation piece. Through Erewhon drink collaborations, a Copenhagen Fashion Week art installation, and “Shower Thoughts”, its interview series featuring creatives and designers, the brand has made a long-ignored item newly desirable.

Nearly five years after launching with a single filtered showerhead, Jolie co-founder and CEO Ryan Babenzien is ready for the brand’s next phase. The beauty and wellness company, which is on track to generate $65 million in revenue in 2026, is introducing its second product on November 11: the Filtered Handheld Showerhead. Available in five of the brand’s signature colorways, including Modern Chrome, Brushed Gold and Vibrant Red, the handheld features a lightweight silhouette, a knurled aluminium handle and a magnetic docking system that allows it to snap into place.

It’s a milestone for a brand that’s built a multi-million-dollar business around a singular hero product, with distribution spanning Erewhon, Ulta Beauty, Costco, and Target. Jolie is among the cohort of brands that have turned mundane products into premium goods, like Touchland, Native, Blueland and Harry’s before it. That approach extends to Jolie’s creative direction, led by co-founder Arjan Singh, who has brought a fashion point of view and an elevated-yet-cheeky filter to the traditionally utilitarian showerhead category. Rather than relying on product imagery, Jolie’s campaigns focus on the feeling and emotion of showering, an otherwise-intimate daily ritual.

Campaign imagery for the Jolie Filtered Showerhead.

The idea began with a personal discovery, Babenzien says. After noticing his skin was unusually dry one winter, Babenzien, who previously founded direct-to-consumer (DTC) footwear brand Greats before selling it to Steve Madden in 2019, began researching the effects of shower water on skin and hair. His spark moment came in the shower, when he realized that a showerhead could be more than a bathroom fixture: it could become a beauty-wellness essential, the first step in a consumer’s daily routine. “Jolie was my ultimate shower thought to date,” Babenzien says, reflecting on the early days of building the brand.

Now, with years of performance proof behind it, Jolie is ready to expand both its product assortment and its awareness. For Valentine’s Day, Jolie partnered with romance publisher 831 Stories on an Instagram series pairing steamy reads with hot showers. In August, during Copenhagen Fashion Week, Jolie installed showers along the city’s harbor for swimmers, bringing the product into a public setting that combined art with function. It also launched campaign films starring Saturday Night Live cast member Veronika Slowikowska, with a preview airing nationally on NBC around SNL’s 52nd season premiere.

Its editorial series, “Shower Thoughts”, also draws inspiration from the bathroom. Originally a written Q&A, it evolved into a video interview series in October, opening with creative director and designer Alex Eagle. Filmed in and around guests’ bathrooms, the series features creatives with distinct points of view who have built something of their own, reflecting Jolie’s ties to fashion, design, art, and culture. Other first-season guests include Vyrao founder Yasmin Sewell and fashion designer Mara Hoffman.

Creative Director Alex Eagle in Jolie’s Shower Thoughts video series.

Together, the campaigns position the shower as a space for reflection, intimacy, and ritual. “Our brand is our focal point and our competitive advantage,” Babenzien says. Now, he wants to ride that to take over the rest of your water supply.

Jolie, named after Babenzien’s wife and the French word for “pretty”, launched in 2022. Before Jolie could build a brand, it had to make the case for the category itself. “I had conviction. I didn’t have certainty, and there’s a difference.”

From the start, Babenzien identified two challenges: educating consumers on why they should filter their shower water and convincing them they could install the product themselves.

To address the first, Jolie licensed publicly available water-quality data and created a free local water report. Users enter their email address and zip code to receive a breakdown of what is in their water, giving the brand a way to explain the potential impact on skin and hair in seconds.

Jolie calls it “step zero”: filtering shower water to reduce chlorine and other contaminants before applying shampoo, conditioner, or skincare. “Beauty and wellness go hand in hand. It’s not one thing; it’s a sequence of things,” Babenzien explains. “It’s what you eat, where you train, what you put in your body, what you put on your body and how you sleep.”

Hair concerns are the biggest initial purchase driver for Jolie, Babenzien says. While hair shedding and thinning can be linked to stress, hormonal changes and postpartum hair loss, the growing use of GLP-1 medications, which have been associated with hair shedding during rapid weight loss, has brought renewed attention to hair health.

Jolie points to clinical testing of its showerhead, reporting that 81% of study participants experienced reduced hair shedding. Skin concerns, including dryness and irritation, are another part of the brand’s appeal. Jolie says clinical testing showed a 50% improvement in skin dryness after four weeks.

Jolie Filtered Showerhead, in Brushed Gold.

Babenzien had planned to expand Jolie’s assortment sooner, but rapid growth of the original showerhead prompted him to hold off. “We’ve always had a product roadmap,” he says. “We decided not to release other products, because the business was growing so quickly and profitably. It didn’t make sense to complicate our operations and supply chain, or to complicate the proposition for the consumer.”

That focus has paid off. Jolie expects to post between $11 million and $12 million in EBITDA in 2026, and says it has processed two million Shopify orders for showerheads and replacement filters since 2021. The company counts 750,000 “daily active users” — Babenzien’s term for customers who use the showerhead as part of their everyday routine — and aims to reach one million by year-end.

Distribution has gone wide — a sign of a shift in strategy from earlier era DTC brands. Jolie launched on Amazon in June 2022, followed by Erewhon in April 2023, Ulta in January 2025, and Costco US in December 2025. In September 2026, it expanded into 600 Target stores. The brand is also stocked in 2,000 hair salons and says more than 10,000 stylists trust and recommend it. Each retail channel requires a different approach to consumer education, from shower-style end-caps at Erewhon to informational displays around Costco pallets.

And nothing signals a brand’s place in the cultural zeitgeist quite like an Erewhon drink collaboration. Jolie and the retailer first partnered on the Spring of Youth iced elixir in 2025, followed by Sacred Water in July 2026. While the first was positively received, Sacred Water proved more polarizing, drawing criticism online and becoming late-night fodder, including in a Jimmy Kimmel Live segment.

Babenzien views the partnership through a brand rather than a revenue lens. For him, even the polarized response demonstrated Jolie’s ability to generate conversation well beyond the showerhead category.

Erewhon helped establish Jolie’s wellness proposition and introduce the brand to a broader retail audience. “Erewhon is a cultural phenomenon and has national influence across all retail in the US,” Babenzien says.

Antoci adds that demand has remained strong since its debut at Erewhon. “Since Erewhon had never sold a product in this category, we were thrilled to see strong customer demand in the first year, and engagement remains high,” he says.

Word of mouth has been critical to Jolie’s growth, Babenzien says, with packaging designed to make the bathroom fixture feel special. The first 10,000 units included a ceramic disc carrying a bespoke fragrance inspired by the waters of Sicily. The brand discontinued it due to overseas shipping complications, but the attention to detail remains, down to a branded wrench and a custom spool of plumber’s tape. Those tools serve a practical purpose, too: addressing Jolie’s second early obstacle by making installation feel like an approachable DIY task rather than a job for a plumber.

Babenzien says Jolie has generated more than 75,000 pieces of user-generated content, helping the business grow without relying entirely on paid marketing. His broader marketing philosophy centers on the idea that “people influence people”, with the aim of making Jolie a topic of conversation at dinner tables, in hair salons and among running groups.

Jolie showerhead art installation at Ofelia Plads, Copenhagen.

The design presented a different challenge: making an everyday fixture distinctive without allowing it to become trend-driven. The team looked to enduring design references including the Rolex Submariner, the Porsche 911, a black tuxedo and the little black dress. “All of these have evolved over decades, but their design identity is clear,” Babenzien says. Those established design codes now carry through to the handheld, which is immediately recognizable as a Jolie product and boasts the same attention to detail.

Its magnetic mount provides a tactile and audible cue when the showerhead is securely docked, making it easier to put back in place. For Babenzien, the experience of removing and replacing it was as important as its filtration function.

As for further product launches in 2027, Babenzien says: “If it’s related to water as it affects your skin, hair and health, it can live in the current Jolie product roadmap.” Next to launch will be a rainfall showerhead, with non-showerhead innovations to come later down the line.

The company has five full-time employees and has grown without institutional capital, the CEO says. While investors have expressed interest, Jolie is not currently raising capital. He remains open to a partner who could help accelerate its next phase of growth.

For now, Babenzien’s priority is managing that growth while keeping Jolie focused. The company is targeting $100 million in revenue in 2027, up from a projected $65 million in 2026.

“The challenge is in our own hands. We have to remain vigilant and focused on the mission, not lose sight of trying to get everybody to filter their shower water, and hopefully get them to do it with a Jolie.”

#6728. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

The best bathrobes for men will turn your modest apartment into a luxury spa in two seconds flat. Sadly, you'll still have to acquire all the relevant permits before you can charge randos for the home massage experience, but that's okay—a swaddly robe is more of a solo thing anyway.

To help you in your quest for relaxation supremacy, we tested a slew of bathrobes to find the best of the best, which you'll find the below. While you're here, be sure to check out our guide to the best pajamas.

If the de facto brand for cool-guy jammies doesn't make you want to cancel your plans and post up at home, its royally fluffy bathrobes will. The only con: limiting yourself to just one.

Dusen Dusen's playful takes on homewares and home decor make it the brand you turn to for something that'll have your houseguests going, “where'd you get that from?” Maybe you won't be wearing a robe in front of said guests, but they can admire its beauty when it's hanging in your bathroom. These printed robes are super plush for post-bath drying sessions, and cozy enough to accidentally fall asleep in while you're sitting on the couch waiting for your hair to dry.

There are robes you dry in, robes you lounge in, and then robes like this: an option meant to live in like you own a McMansion, smoke cigars every night, and enjoy a dram of scotch to “take the edge off.” This Derek Rose cotton robe has a satin-like finish, with a subtle stripe detail that gives it more of a pop than just a regular old blue colorway. So imagine our delight when Canada's foremost fleece whizzes brought their particular set of skills to the humble bathroom robe, juicing up the silhouette in the same loopback cotton-jersey that makes their loungewear so great. Wear this terry cloth robe while catching up on the Great British Bake Off from the comfort of your couch—and to make the inevitable trip to the grocery store for miscellaneous pie ingredients immediately afterwards.

This is type of robe you throw on when you want to toast things up but have zero plans to leave the house and therefore refuse to put on "actual" clothes. It has a sweet shawl collar and a full length that gives you all the cozy coverage you want.

What's better than sleeping on a cloud? Being swaddled in one while you slowly meander aorund your apartment. The Parachute robe offers a barely there feel, made possible thanks to its four-ply gauze construction. This one has side-seam pockets that make it easy to slip into

Hommey's catalog of cheerful colors and patterns help the brand stand out, but they're more than just nice to look at. A Purple Label look, for Polo prices. Thank you, Ralph.

Material: A lot of fabric is about to touch your naked body, so you better make sure your robe feels good. Take advantage of any size guides to really help you lock in your correct sizing.

Testing robes is no easy feat. We had to strip down to our skivvies, throw on a bunch of cozy options, and, well, chill. We made note of each robe's comfort factor, which usually had to do with the material of the robe. All of the robes we featured here are sure to suit the preference of basically anyone who would ever shop for a robe, whether they want a hood, prefer something to keep them dry and warm after a shower, or just lounge in like a baller.
