#6724. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6721. K-Beauty Brand Anua Cracked TikTok. What’s Next?

Cutting through the crowded K-beauty market takes a special mix of product innovation and social media savvy, which very few manage to achieve. But for seven-year-old Anua, a viral concoction of Korean botanical formulas, sleek branding and a hint of star power (from Kendall Jenner) has helped the brand break through globally this year.

There are currently more than half a million posts featuring the #Anua hashtag on TikTok, including product reviews from the likes of Mexican beauty creator Mireya Rios (five million followers) and application walkthroughs by celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips (461,700 followers), garnering over seven billion views altogether. The brand’s most recent success, though, is its collaboration with Netflix animation — and cultural phenomenon — KPop Demon Hunters, thought up by the brand’s co-founder and CEO Changju Lee, and overseen by recently appointed CMO Michelle Miller.

“It’s been a wild six months,” Miller says over Zoom from her LA base (the rest of Anua’s in-house team remains in Seoul). Miller started at Anua in April 2026, arriving from cult haircare label K18 where she worked as founding CMO. “The growth has been very fast. We’re now a top 10 brand in earned media value globally and top four in the US.”

Left to right: PDRN Hyaluronic Acid Cream, Heartleaf Cleansing Oil, Heartleaf Quercetinol Cleansing Foam, Azelaic Acid 10 Serum, Heartleaf 77 Soothing Toner. Photo: Courtesy of Anua

Anua launched in Seoul in 2019 with its Heartleaf 77% Soothing Toner ($21). The skin-soothing, anti-inflammatory properties of its hero heartleaf ingredient broke through the market, responding precisely to the white space its co-founders Lee and Seonhyeong Yi, whose paths crossed at Seoul National University, identified pre-launch.

Anua’s current range is in hot demand. The Founders Inc., the brand’s parent company, which was founded by Lee and Yi in 2017 and is entirely self-funded, reported 68% year-on-year revenue growth in 2025. The company did not share how much was generated by Anua, but in the portfolio, it sits alongside the founders’ first venture, Project 21, a pet lifestyle brand, as well as dermatological haircare label Fromlabs.

“When we began exploring the market, we found that consumers were often overwhelmed by complicated routines and products that didn’t always address their everyday skin concerns,” Lee says. “Our research pointed to a clear need: effective, gentle skincare at a reasonable price that people can easily incorporate into their daily lives.”

This early focus on simplifying a category associated with science-led ingredients — unknown and, in some cases, unsafe to the average drugstore skincare user — helped Anua get its foothold in an already-bustling K-beauty business. But the turning point was when the brand branched out beyond its hero heartleaf line to respond to what the customer wanted next. Soon came the Niacinamide 10% + TXA 4% Serum ($22), an active formula still focused on gentle and guided application, followed by its Azelaic Acid 10% Serum ($22) and PDRN line ($21-$28) featuring a cream and a hyaluronic acid serum (Jenner’s favorite). The PDRN cream ranked #1 in the facial moisturizer category on Amazon US in September, Lee shares.

Anua hosted its first Dew on the Go pop-up in New York in June to celebrate its PDRN line. Photo: Courtesy of Anua

After gaining steam on TikTok Shop and Amazon — Anua prides itself on being “digitally native” — Anua broke into the real-life retail space with Ulta Beauty in the US in February 2025, where it now ranks among the retailer’s top five skincare brands. As for the rest of its physical doors (there are over 40,000 globally), it can be found in Sephoras worldwide, as well as UK multi-brand stores spanning Selfridges to Boots.

However, competing in the K-beauty race is not easy. It is a trend-led category with a new disrupter brand seemingly each week, from Medicube to Beauty of Joseon and Cosrx, all reaching for virality through innovation and a rapid speed-to-market. The online K-beauty market was worth $15 billion globally in 2025, up from $12.5 billion a year prior, according to Euromonitor International. And then there’s the question of category longevity: the possibility that another breakthrough market, like Chinese C-beauty or Scandi beauty, might bubble up and take K-beauty’s steam (China made up 21% of online K-beauty sales globally in 2025, per Euromonitor, down from 66% a year earlier).

How is Anua planning to compete and stay the course? Its next phase, Lee says, is about keeping customer acquisition flowing, while converting its current customers from trend-led purchasers to loyal brand fans.

To pin down the KPop Demon Hunters partnership, Lee reached out to Netflix personally to secure the IP for the year and then pitched the campaign to Ulta, acquiring additional shelf space across the brand’s US stores and claiming premium merchandising spots, where footfall is higher.

The rise of Korean culture, from K-pop to K-dramas, has played a big role in boosting K-beauty globally, with more consumers looking to adopt trends inspired by their favorite stars. The Netflix hit offered Anua the perfect opening, says Miller. “It was such a natural tie-in. When KPop Demon Hunters saw wild success globally, especially in the US market, it was a really proud moment for Korea. And for us, it’s a cultural intersection that we can tap into,” she says. “People are just eating up Korean culture, and wanting more.”

The year-long campaign, which runs through February 2027, includes a short film shot by K-pop music video director Kylie Kang that translates the franchise’s storyline — a fictional girl group who double as pop idols and supernatural demon slayers — to fighting everyday skin woes. Accompanying 48-hour pop-ups took place in October at two of Ulta Beauty’s LA outposts — Santa Monica and Westwood — resulting in snaking queues and surpassing sales targets by more than 62%, according to Miller.

The limited-edition KPop Demon Hunters range on sale at the brand’s Ulta Beauty activation in LA. Photo: Courtesy of Anua

However, KPop Demon Hunters is predominantly associated with an audience as young as 10, and some of Anua’s bestsellers are stocked with active ingredients. How is it avoiding the promotion of harsh formulas for vulnerable skin? “In the collection for KPop, we exclusively have pimple patches, a really gentle sheet mask, a sunscreen — so barrier-protecting products that can translate across different skin,” Miller explains, adding that it’s also helping the brand widen its consumer base. “It’s allowed us to capture both moms and their daughters, which is not a bad place to be.”

Beyond cultural tie-ins, creator-led marketing is leading the way. “Our most valuable marketing investment has been building our creator community,” says CEO Lee. “From the beginning, we invested in getting products into the hands of consumers and creators who could share their experiences. That approach helped us build credibility, drive discovery, and better understand what consumers wanted.”

With trust in traditional influencers slowly dwindling, Anua continues to adopt a tiered approach to seeding (the sending of free product samples to influencers without a paid contract to post). “We seed a lot, and we have different layers of that,” Miller explains. “We have seeding efforts through our TikTok Shop affiliates. We have wider seeding efforts to micro-creators, or to those who are more niche, like a specific college community or a nurse. And then we have our more strategic seeding of top creators. At the end of the day, people trust people, and that’s what converts.”

How does the brand decide who it works with? “When you work with the volume of creators that we do, it’s about looking at it from a few different lenses. First, we need to reach a trifecta of different creators, so people with different skin tones, skin problems, personas, ages. Then, we have a great community of experts, such as dermatologists and makeup artists, that really builds trust. And finally, we have people like Kendall [Jenner], who are moving culture.”

Jenner was announced as Anua’s first-ever global brand ambassador in June, which felt like the natural next step, says Lee. “As Anua scales, we’re maintaining our investment in grassroots creators while expanding into global partnerships, experiential marketing, and integrated retail campaigns. Our partnership with Kendall represents this next stage, introducing Anua to a global audience,” he says. The campaign shines light on the brand’s viral PDRN line, which Jenner already had an affinity for, according to Miller; the model’s makeup artist, Phillips, uses the PDRN cream as part of her viral underpainting technique, where the face is contoured prior to applying foundation.

Beyond acquisition, the bigger challenge is building loyalty, says Lee, which is where listening comes in. “We use consumer data, social listening, customer reviews, and direct feedback to identify emerging needs and develop products around them,” he explains. Miller agrees that listening is the brand’s edge. “I’d say our playbook has always been to start with the customer, really listen to the customer, and I think social media has provided new ways of doing that,” she adds.

Outside the Dew on the Go event in SoHo. Photo: Courtesy of Anua

This includes product review videos — positive or negative. “Consumer feedback is central to how we operate. Because Anua was built digitally, we’ve always had a close connection with our customers, monitoring ratings, written feedback, and social conversations to understand what’s working and where we can improve,” says Lee. “Those insights have led us to reformulate products, develop new ones, and adjust our marketing direction.” The brand decided to create a new, milder version of its bestselling Heartleaf Cleansing Oil based on customer feedback, with fewer ingredients better tailored to sensitive skin.

What it comes down to, though, is reacting to what consumers want in real time, to stay on top of a fast-moving market. For example, the brand launched an azelaic acid serum in December 2024, having noticed an uptick in searches for the ingredient. The Azelaic Acid 10% Serum is currently Ulta Beauty’s top-selling serum. “We were early to that trend, and were able to create a formulation people really want,” Miller says, flagging that, as with any active ingredient the brand rolls out, education is key. “We have our dermatologist and expert community to explain what ‘10% active’ means [on social media], how to use it, when, and what the best skin type is for that.”

As Anua works to build a full regime that customers return to year after year, pushing beyond one or two viral bestsellers, it is flexing its retail muscles. The brand rolled out in 40 physical SpaceNK stores in September, as well as Selfridges in the summer, where it hosted dedicated retail pop-ups across London, Birmingham and Manchester. “Our biggest opportunity is evolving Anua from a viral K-beauty brand into a globally recognized skincare label that will be around in a long time. We know creator marketing is a big part of that, but it’s also about leaning into retail, real-life experiences, and just building a whole ecosystem of Anua,” Miller says.

Celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips hosts a masterclass in LA, using the brand’s PDRN products. Photo: Courtesy of Anua

For Lee, this comes with a new set of challenges. “One of our biggest challenges has been evolving from a digitally native brand into a global organization operating across different markets, retail environments, and consumer cultures,” he says. “The strategies that drive growth online don’t always translate directly into physical retail. Each market requires a deeper understanding of local consumers, shopping habits, and commercial dynamics.”

To drive growth, it needs stronger teams with new expertise, as well as the infrastructure to support a larger business, he continues. “We’ve had to balance that operational discipline with the speed and entrepreneurial mindset that helped build Anua,” he says. Lee also plans to keep listening to consumers to determine his next steps. “We assess expansion through the consumer’s experience: can they easily find the product they want, understand its benefits, and buy it through a retailer they trust? Building a global brand means delivering on those expectations consistently.”

As for the ultimate goal, Lee says something surprising for a brand operating in one of the buzziest markets. “We’re proud of our Korean heritage, but we don’t want to be defined solely as a K-beauty brand,” he says. “We want to be recognized for innovation, performance and trust; one that is still relevant and thriving 100 years from now.”

#6720. The 15 Best Chelsea Boots for Men in 2026: Never Go Out of Style

The best Chelsea boots for men are trend-proof in a way that'll make you breathe a sigh of relief. Especially right now, when menswear feels like a WWE Royal Rumble, where anything goes and trends pile up like bodies in and out of the ring. But there, floating confidently above everything, is the trustworthy Chelsea boot.

If we had to make an educated guess as to why the Chelsea boot has stuck around for so long? Good design is good design. The slip-on simplicity, the sharp silhouette, the unadorned, uncomplicated details—the pared-back design makes it highly adaptable to any wardrobe and occasion, trends be damned. So don't be ashamed to cash in on a fleeting fad, but when it comes time for you to do some spring cleaning, we'd advise against letting go of a pair of Chelseas.

We've rounded up 15 of the best Chelsea boots out there, from hardwearing stompers to exquisite stunners, $200 steals to $1,500 beauties. Finding the perfect pair can be hard—but pulling them on? Easy.

Ask us what Chelsea boot you should get, regardless of price, and we'll point to the R.M. Williams Turnout boot, because it does so many things right that the competition can't. Off the bat, it’s a real stunner. The silhouette is sleek and chiseled, timeless and fashion forward. The leather is perfectly suited for a shine and polish to attend any black tie event, but takes on a handsome patina when worn hard. Plus, the quality is fantastic. The wholecut leather uppers are shaped as a single piece of cowhide rather than several panels stitched together, resulting in a shoe that’s as pretty as it is durable. With Goodyear-welted construction for easy peasy resoling, you’ll have these Aussie-born boots for well over a decade.

How does a boot originally built for Down Under cowboys manage to be the best-looking dress boot and hardest-wearing boot at the same time? Hard to say. The only drawback of the R.M. Williams Heritage Craftsman Chelsea is the price. But considering everything it can do—and how long it'll last—the math makes sense.

For the budget conscious/the dude looking for his first pair of “nice” Chelsea boots, my answer is easy: Beckett Simonon. Menswear bros might scoff at a web-only DTC clothing brand, but unlike the other brands with infinite marketing budgets looking to “disrupt the entire industry”, Beckett Simonon seems content with making great shoes at a great price, without all the soulless millennial pandering. The Bolton, a slick sleek, true-to-form  Chelsea boot, is just the poster child for the brand’s modus operandi. It uses full-grain Italian calfskin, which is lined with Vachetta leather, stitched by master shoemakers in Columbia using a Blake stitch construction.

In other words, it’s a Chelsea boot with A-list looks, Northamptonshire-style pedigree, and a price that’s at least half of the competition. But if there’s one thing that will stop most people from buying a pair immediately is, well, you can’t get them immediately. Each pair is made to order, which means you’ll have to wait a month or two to get yours. But you know what they say: patience is a virtue.

Some Chelsea boots lean heavily into their rockstar appeal, while others skew utilitarian, expressly designed to protect you from the elements. Then there, however, are the rare pairs that gracefully straddle the line between. Enter the other Australian boot: Blundstone. Those tough leather uppers might not be monsoon-ready, but on days when you just need to jump a few puddles en route to work, the whole package is the slickest way to ensure your socks stay dry without compromising your fit.

Tired Bushwick memes aside, Blunnies are truly good looking boots built like a tank. They can take a real whooping and still show up for their 5 a.m. shift behind the espresso machine, ready for more. They’re a boot you don’t have to feel precious about, and the de facto kicks to wear when the weather forecast just says “shitty.” They look great with vintage jeans, a pair of Dickies, cargo pants, and chinos—though, in our humble opinion, they don't belong anywhere with a dress code (explicit or implied).

Hedi Slimane’s legacy at Saint Laurent was all skinny jeans, razor-sharp suits, and rockstar Chelsea boots. The look he cooked up over a decade ago has come back again, with guys dubbing themselves Hedi Boys looking to recreate the magic. One glance at boots like these, and you understand why. A leading man gleam and a stacked Cuban heel mean these boots by themselves could headline Coachella. The only update: a very right-now edginess (literally) at the toe. Whether or not the rumored skinny jeans comeback arrives, these are the boots to wear when you want all eyes on you.

Astorflex has long been one of the best value propositions in the shoe space. The Tuscan vegetable-tanned leather and multigenerational craftsmanship alone should be worth more than what you'll actually pay. But value doesn't equate to style. Thankfully, the Bitflex has that in spades. Not too pointy and not totally bulbous, the shape splits the difference masterfully and looks great paired with any kind of pants. Plus, the cushioned crepe sole plays down the dressy factor while adding a ton of comfort straight out of the box.

Unlike other crepe-soled boots more famous than these—ahem—these don’t feel suspiciously soft, despite their extremely comfortable feel. In my experience, Astorflex boots maintain great arch support and mold to your feet, but also are built up enough to provide some noticeable ankle support. This is certainly the most casual Chelsea boot here, so don’t even think of trying to wear these to your friend’s wedding. You’re not “doing something”, you’re being disrespectful.

If you think of Red Wing, it's the brand’s iconic 6-inch moc toe boots you’re probably imagining. But the Minnesotan boot makers can do more than turn out jobsite-endorsed footwear. Introduced in the 1990s, Red Wing’s Chelseas were made for ranchers who wanted something durable enough for the farm, but easy enough to nap in. They’re a happy middle ground between a high-shine European Chelsea like the R.M. Williams and the woodsy Blundstones.

That means you get Goodyear-welted construction and built-to-stroll rubber outsoles topped by Hawthorne Muleskinner roughout suede. The texture is “rugged handyman,” but the dusty tan and dark brown color can hold down a coffee date-worthy fit. White tees and white jeans? Sure. Nice pants and a knit sweater or polo? Absolutely. Wranglers and a Stetson. Of course.

Morjas is best known for loafers worn by everyone from Wall Street bros to Greenpoint baristas. Now the Swedish shoemakers are coming for your ankles with a Chelsea boot. If you’ve already graduated from Chelsea Boots 101 by having a classic black or brown calf-leather pair in your closet, consider these brown suede beauties for next semester.

They're fully leather-lined but require absolutely zero break-in time, thanks to a studded rubber sole that feels like walking on a cloud... if clouds had traction. Style-wise, they walk the line (pun intended) between office-ready and weekend cool—equally dialed in when paired with a crisp white dress shirt beneath unforgiving Monday-morning fluorescents or some linen pants while you sip a doppia espresso in Florence.

You already know what that yellow stitching means. Dr. Martens’ chunky, iconic boots bring an EVA insole and the brand's patented oil- and slip-resistant AirWair sole to the water-resistant oiled leather. Add a pull tab for easy entry, and the only thing easier than slipping them on is adding them to cart when you realize they’re on sale.

By cutting out the middleman and selling direct-to-consumer, Meermin offers handsome, Goodyear-welted dress shoes—all made from leather with absurdly tony provenances—for well below what the other guys charge. You can’t go wrong with any of the brand’s boots, but a mocha-hued suede Chelsea looks especially killer in the fall.

Blundstones again, you say? Well, yes. But this pair has a leather lining and plusher sole, which make them both more comfortable and longer lasting, if for a slightly higher price.

From the rugged to the refined. Chelsea boots are named after London's affluent Chelsea neighbourhood, and this model from British quality shoemakers Crockett & Jones' lives up to that name perhaps more than any on this list.

The Spanish shoe-whisperers at Camper fly a little under the radar compared to their British counterparts, but their Chelsea boots offer just as much swaggering rock-god energy as any other pair on this list. Thanks to a cushy OrthoLite footbed, though, you can wear ‘em long after Mick Jagger takes his final bow.

The chatter about Our Legacy's Camion boots never seems to end. That handsome silhouette, the '90s-esque square toe, and the slick side zip make these a modern-day classic.

Viberg makes boots on steroids in its family-owned Canadian factory, turning out museum-worthy footwear designed to stomp through the worst the world—or the ground, at least—has to offer. These Chelseas are cut from a single piece of waxed leather, like a Barbour jacket for your feet.

NYC-based 3sixteen has been on an absolute footwear tear lately—first with its slick Saucony collab, and now with a lug-soled Chelsea boot that stands on business. The whole shoe smashes together slightly disparate details—an elegant tobacco-colored suede, a workmanlike wedge lugged sole, an skyscraper-height ankle—that add up to something fresh in the normally staid world of Chelsea boots. And if you’ve ever broken in a pair of 3sixteen’s top-tier jeans, you already know: things only get better as you put in the steps.

Chelsea boots have always looked cool—anywhere, on anyone, at any time. They were invented in the 1800s, but won their cultural cred later: the Beatles gave them a massive co-sign in the ’60s, then Hedi Slimane anchored his Saint Laurent rocker suits with them while rappers stacked their denim on top of Chelsea boots during the 2010s.

Which goes to show that Chelsea boots work with damn near anything in your closet, from your favorite Levi’s to baggy chinos to louche suits—even crew socks and shorts, depending on the boots and your taste for channeling some Pacific Northwest crunchiness. For more, check out our guide on how to wear Chelsea boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6719. Meghan Markle Made a Subtle Change to Her Wedding Jewelry for a European Parliament Visit

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry visited the European Parliament in Brussels today to usher in the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial, which honors children who lost their lives after suffering harm from social media. For the solemn occasion, the Duchess of Sussex kept her look minimal, including her accessories and wedding stack. Meghan only wore her Welsh gold wedding band on her left ring finger, forgoing her engagement ring.

Meghan has a history of wearing just her wedding band while on trips abroad. Still, the piece is nearly priceless itself due to its material.

“Very little Welsh gold was ever mined, and it is traditionally used to make the British royal family’s wedding bands,” Hera Fine Jewelry founder and CEO Lauren Boc previously told ELLE while discussing Kate Middleton’s wedding stack. “Between its natural rarity and historic connections, I would consider her Welsh gold wedding band to be close to invaluable.”

Meghan accessorized her black Mackage coat with a few other gold pieces this morning, including her vintage Dior crystal earrings and Cartier Love bracelet.

Meghan has no other upcoming events that have been announced. Last month, following the Sussexes’ visit to Nottingham, a source close to the couple told The Telegraph that Meghan rarely joins Harry for engagements.

“They have different professional priorities,” one source explained. “Prince Harry’s is his philanthropic work and public service. Her focus is on her family and children, followed by her business, followed by rebooting her acting career. Her public appearances will be relatively rare. She is reading a lot of scripts at the moment. If she has time left after all of that, she will do some charity work. But she’s not a working royal; her day isn’t organized around a program pulled together by a private secretary. She’s a full-time mom and entrepreneur, and that alone takes up a lot of time and work.”

#6718. Three Prada Obsessives Unpack Miuccia’s Defining Decade

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Bazaar’s Lynette Nylander and Camille Freestone join Laia Garcia-Furtado for a roundtable on her new book, Prada in the Nineties

Prada is as much an adjective as it is a noun. My colleagues and I often describe wardrobe twists, like a bejeweled brooch on a Peter Pan collar or an embroidered sock peeking out of a Mary Jane, as “very Prada.” But what is it about these little notes of character that signals “Prada” in our brain?

That’s one of the questions Bazaar’s deputy culture director, Laia Garcia-Furtado, answers in her new book, Prada in the Nineties. (Published by Batsford, it drops today.) Her deep dive into one of the brand’s most pivotal decades reaches far beyond the heroin-chic label we tend to slap on ’90s fashion. From runway reviews to cultural anecdotes, Garcia-Furtado takes us backstage, into the life and personality of Miuccia Prada, the industry’s north star of intellectual fashion.

Mrs. Prada’s arsenal of off-color prints and skirts have inspired generations of women to aspire to an ugly-chic kind of cool; looking at her today, it’s easy to find ourselves lost in her world. But in harkening back to the nascent stages of her career as a designer, Garcia-Furtado reminds us that the throughline of her genius lies in her sense of self.

It’s a story that began with nylon, an unexpected choice for a member of the Prada family, with its legacy of selling bespoke leather goods to royal clientele. Yet Mrs. Prada’s choice to bring nylon totes and duffels to the luxury market was not merely driven by rebellion—it was a manifestation of her own desire for a well-designed bag that embraced utility. And the groundbreaking success of the bags demonstrated that her dreams were shared by other women—a hint of where Prada would take the brand.

Garcia-Furtado understands this lore firsthand. After all, she’s spent a lot of time in Mrs. Prada’s shoes—well, the ones she designed, at least. She began building her own archive of Miuccia merch in college with a pair of woven leather Mary Janes by Prada’s little sister, Miu Miu. A lucky eBay find from the spring 2001 collection, they were marked by interlaced checks of leather with pops of plum purple and canvas buckle straps. She has continued to build her collection ever since.

Writing the book gave Garcia-Furtado carte blanche to dig into the nitty-gritty details that unite women of varying tastes and lifestyles as proud members of Prada’s hive. Below, she gathers with Bazaar’s fellow Prada obsessees, executive digital director Lynette Nylander and senior fashion writer Camille Freestone, to unpack all the things that have placed Mrs. Prada in a league of her own, from the ’90s to now.

Jennifer Jenkins: What inspired you to go on such a deep dive on Miuccia Prada?

Laia Garcia-Furtado: There are very specific images that we go to when we think of Prada in the ’90s, but all of those collections are from the late ’90s. So I thought, "Wait, what about the early '90s?" When I started looking up those collections, I realized that what I was really doing was tracing how Prada went from almost an independent, fledgling designer to an icon in a period of ten years, which is really crazy. I love to go down a research hole; that's actually my favorite thing. It was just great to have an excuse.

Lynette Nylander: One of the things that struck me about going through Laia’s book, and my own personal understanding of Prada in the '90s, is that it was really foundational. A lot of the signatures and markers of what Prada is today were made in that formative time. One of my favorite things about being part of the Prada hive—and I think we all identify as that—is that she has carefully constructed a brand where you can mine from its past. She's very okay with the idea that something is a rehashed idea from a '90s collection in the 2000s, in the 2010s, in the 2020s. Everything is meant to be in dialogue with everything else. That's really refreshing in a world where designers are making very distinct collections and basically almost asking you to do away with whatever you bought last year and buy into what's “now.” She very much respects the past, which is why I think a book on the '90s is brilliant.

Camille Freestone: Also, the designs are so pared back. We think now of much more heavy-handed embellishment when we imagine Prada. Part of it was that it was the '90s and it was just a simpler time. Runways have just gotten more megawatt altogether. But the Prada collections are quite pure. The design is quite simple in the best way, so they let her creative touches shine in such a way that feels very present.

LGF: I mean everything old is new, et cetera. Going back to what you were saying about the simple shapes, even when things are heavily embellished and there's a lot of beading and sequins, it never feels like putting on a bunch of stuff for the sake of putting on a bunch of stuff. Even if it's super over-the-top, you think, “It's exactly what it needs to be.” It feels very real. One of my favorite things I read while I was doing research is a quote where she's saying how in movies and in art, you're allowed to bring in real life and it's allowed to be ugly and regular, but fashion was a place where you weren't allowed to do that, and she wanted to change that. When I read that, everything from those old collections made so much sense.

But even now, I think you can read a collection, even if she and Raf are saying that it's about one thing, and you look at it, you're like, "It's really about something else."

LN: Yeah, and that's always been a part of that duality. And I mean, even in the inception of Miu Miu, she talks about it as this other side of her personality. She's someone who is really in dialogue with her more fantastical, imagined self. And I think what was interesting about going through the '90s collections was that it was fantastical, but again, more real.

But I want to talk about what you learned. They always say hindsight is 20/20, but I don't think we were lucky enough to understand what a unique time the ‘90s were. It was pre-social-media. Celebrity culture had hit this apex, and Miuccia was there as this brand that carried and collected a lot of celebrity in a way that is not how it is now.

LGF: It wasn’t grody! And I think that was especially evident when she launched menswear, and John Malkovich was her model or Willem Dafoe—I mean, now we all love Willem Dafoe, of course, but it was very different from what everyone else was doing.

And another thing that's really interesting is that we have a vision of the ’90s, but the first couple of years of the ‘90s are still the ’80s. It takes years for the prevailing aesthetic that we all remember to rise up. Going back, Prada was a heritage label, but she launched ready-to-wear in the late ‘80s. And it wasn't like when Vuitton launched ready-to-wear, when everybody understood it as a major brand. Prada was by no means in its flop era, but it wasn’t as well known as Vuitton. It was not the same.

So when she started, critics were writing things like “Prada also showed a collection.” There wasn't even a long review. And then she sort of started getting talked about in the same breath as Martin Margiela or Ann Demeulemeester, like, “These people are the plucky new designers.” We think she's so untouchable now and it's like she almost can do no wrong, but you can go back and see how it all started and see her be like, "I hated this collection actually, and I'll never do that again.” I mean, my kingdom for any designer that would say that now—to just be that honest.

JJ: You touched a lot on her unapologetic way of expressing herself, even while taking in different cultural references and touchpoints. Was there anything in particular you were most surprised to learn about her?

LGF: My favorite trivia is that she got married on Valentine's Day.

LGF: She's a romantic. I feel like that says so much.

CF: It's amazing. She was in the Communist Party of Italy, and so not of the fashion world at all, but so endlessly fascinated by it.

LGF: It's so funny because it's very much like her parents said, "Okay, you've had your fun. Now, come back home, join the family business.” And she wanted to be an actor—the mime thing! In one interview, she said, "My favorite part was when we had to do really specific body control stuff." And you can totally see her just being so good at that.

LN: Well, I think that she's so good at it because I can't think of a designer, at least in more modern history, that really sort of mines from herself. Have you ever noticed, if you read a part of a review, or you’ve seen those videos of her backstage, it's never like, "I was looking at the art of Georgia O’Keeffe”?

LN: She doesn't even mine it from a place. She isn't even saying, "Oh, I was walking down the piazza in Milan." It's not about that—it's this higher sense of self. I think about the fall/winter 2026 collection, with Bella Hadid and the four rounds of looks. And of course she did that because she's the only person who would do that, because those are the things that ticktock around in the caverns of her mind when we're all fast asleep.

CF: Well, she's oddly practical. She's kind of utilitarian. And I think now I'm just saying a different thing in different words, but you think of a crystal embellishment when you think of Prada, you think of a quirk, but it's all rooted in a really utilitarian approach. I feel like this is clothing, not art.

LGF: It's also because that's how she dresses. I mean, yes, are her high heels too high for us to walk and not get blisters? Yes, but we still wear them. It's fine. But she designs clothes that she wants to wear, and we always look at what she's wearing at the end of the show to see how she's styling.

LN: She's the model that we're looking for at the end of the show.

CF: Then it's funny to put her back in dialogue with a Martin Margiela; they both were subversive in their own ways, but hers was lensed through an idea that these are just clothes. You need to get dressed in them!

LGF: There is something about the two of them. Margiela never wanted to be interviewed, but when you look back at a lot of the profiles of her, there will be editorials where it's designers with their muses, and she's almost always by herself. She's her own muse.

It's just her. It's like her looking in a mirror. It's her and her son, or it's her by herself, but it's such a clear vision. And I mean, I think it also makes a difference because a lot of the male designers need a muse… but for her, it's always her.

CF: I'm also always fascinated by the “designer uniform.” There are so many examples. Phoebe Philo, Michael Kors, Jonathan Anderson: everyone takes their bow, and it's almost like they're the antithesis of their clothes. So obviously, we are always talking about a woman designing for women, but in that particular context of those big houses, she's one of the few who is just dressing just like her collection.

LGF: And it's amazing the few times she's come out wearing pants.

LGF: It's so rare! You're like, "Oh my god, the slim cigarette.”

LN: I have two things I want to say to the idea that she doesn't really have a muse. The muse is herself, but somehow that doesn't come across as arrogant. It's not the opposite. It comes across as, “I just do what I know I’ll respond to and hopefully other people like it.” And I think there's something really earnest about it.

CF: There's also no ideal of the perfect woman, either.

LN: Yes, in fact, I don't think she even really deals or trades in ideals.

I also want to talk about the colors. I mean, if I think about Prada, I just think about this kaleidoscopic universe of color. She can go anywhere. She can put any color combination together. It's kind of genius. But particularly in the '90s… they're all quite muted. You have this line from Robin Givhan in the book, “The greens hovered somewhere between shades of slime and mold. The browns were”—I mean, this is the beauty of the Robin Givhan written line—“the browns were murky, the color of water as it stagnates over a long, steamy summer. The dizzy and crisscross patterns were reminiscent of UHF static or an old-fashioned labyrinth in rusted plumbing.”

LGF: It's funny though because she hated all of those collections.

LN: I think if there was ever going to be a brand that's going to respect the fact that Robin Givhan ripped her to shreds, it's going to be her. I think she believes in the idea of free thought, and that was Givhan’s thought and put so beautifully.

But I do want to talk about the colors, because I just think it's so specific of how I think about Prada, but also how I think about my own relationship to color. I don't know if you feel like that, but probably in an inadvertent way, she has given me the confidence and the permission to put together these really disparate color combinations.

LGF: I mean, I think that collection that Robin is talking about, from spring ’96 (which is the root cause of my everything; I had a slime green room—I love slime green) is really interesting. Even before she got into the cool color combinations that we know her from, those early '90s collections, even when it was like, “Here's a bunch of beautiful white dresses,” suddenly there would be weird goldenrod silk and a weird orange. The color thing was always there from the beginning. And when you look at the collections throughout the years, you see how she gets a little bit more confident in that and starts mixing it. But that punch of weirdness was present from the beginning.

CF: But somehow, I think, "Why do I like this slime shade? Why do I like this brown? Why do I like this purple?" But all of a sudden, she's made me want purple.

LN: I hate purple in any other context than hers—I need purple.

CF: All of a sudden I want purple. And there's these weird plaids that all of a sudden make me think, "Oh, I need that."

LGF: Also, in the late '90s, she does collections with things embellished with mirrors, and she was like, "Well, everyone is being a hippie and doing this, so I also did it,” but she did it extra crazy. And I love when she is engaging.

Going back to what you said about her being probably one of the few designers that is like, "This review panned me, it's fine,” I feel like she really was engaging with what was being written about her.

One season editors were like, "There are no suits. This is outrageous! Where are all the suits?" So then the next season she opened the collection with a suit and it's very like, "You're welcome. Are you happy now?” I like to see her engage, not that she doesn't do that anymore, but I think in the ’90s, it was a little bit more obvious.

LN: And now she kind of hovers above it all. I want to talk about 1998. Her ascent was complete, you say, in 1998, when she was now at over a half a billion dollars in sales. She landed at 15 in Vogue’s list of the most influential brands. Other women at the top 20 were Donna Karan, Angela Missoni, and Krizia’s Mariuccia Mandelli, and Miuccia is one of the only working designers left. What was happening in 1998, and what collection is that?

LGF: It's the one with the cool red-and-white boots that are space-age. It's all very space-age mod. ‘98 is the time when she went all-in on the millennial aesthetic that everyone was into, when she did her sports thing.

CF: I also think she doesn't deal very much in volume. That's not really her game.

LN: Thank god. I don't know if I'd want a poofy Prada.

LGF: Yeah. But it's so crazy—in a decade you go from reviews that say, "Oh, Prada also showed a collection," to, "Everyone is focused on whatever she does."

LGF: I think she just became more confident in her vision, which was different from everyone else. And I mean, Tom Ford was also doing something at Gucci; there was that vibe shift, and she was part of it, but it was different. From the beginning, she was always the thinking woman's sex-appeal designer, and that just stayed. She was very in tune with the culture, but she wasn't just doing reproductions of what you could see. She was injecting it with her own aesthetic.

You can look at something and say, "Oh, this was her way of doing grunge," but it was not grunge. It was her own thing.

LN: What was that thing? I mean, do you look at broader context and get a sense of the music she listens to or the boys she kissed or the movies she liked?

LGF: Yeah, I think it's very much a movies thing. I feel like you get a sense of her upbringing. The Mary Jane—the shoes she wore as a little girl—were always a thing. She got married in a dress and a coat made by a childrenswear designer. The little socks—you start seeing those reflections of her life, and they're more apparent the more that you know her, but I don't think it's the kind of thing where you need to know what it is in order to like it. And I think there is something about it where it's for grown women. Young people also like it, but her clothes are not clothes for young teen girls.

LN: Was that also something you learned from your research?

LGF: I mean, technically, I think Miu Miu was supposed to be the younger brand, and the vibe did feel a little bit younger, but Prada always felt a little bit adult. Even when you look at the suits or the proper little silk dresses, you're like, "These are clothes for adults."

CF: I feel like that's also where the styling sneaks in. You’ll see the childlike Mary Jane with the suit and maybe one little brooch or something that is so subtle…but it's not hitting you over the head.

LGF: Yeah, because I think there's also a thing where you always look up to something. You know how you read Seventeen magazine when you're 12? And I think there is something about Prada where no matter how old you are, it still feels just beyond where you currently are.

LN: Every time I buy a piece, it still feels, in a weird way, unattainable, or I question if I'm mature or smart or cool enough.

LGF: And then you look in the mirror, and it feels like it feels exactly where you should be.

CF: It is like, "Am I a woman? Am I a glamorous woman?"

LN: Yeah. Maybe it's just because we think about her so much as the likeness of that.

CF: Well, we have made her the ideal almost. She is the one to be judged against, for so many people, but then that makes it hard to articulate what she actually is.

LGF: But even her glamour—there is something attainable about it. She doesn't wear crazy makeup, and she doesn't style her hair in any kind of way. It's just her holding her little scarf, and you think, "I need a scarf to hold!" Going back to her interest in real life, it's just so her. And who doesn't want to just be like themselves? You want to be her, but you really just want to be you.

#6717. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6716. At This New Retreat on a Windswept Estonian Island, You Can Experience Five Seasons of Wellness

You’ve heard of spring, summer, fall, and winter. But what about viies aastaaeg? Across the islands of western Estonia in late March, as the ice thaws and the Baltic mists shift, a micro-season is created—one that Eha, a new retreat on the remote island of Hiiumaa which opened in early October, has termed “springrise” and placed at the center of its “five seasons” wellness philosophy. “Hiiumaa has its own rhythm,” says the Tallinn-born Eva Maran, who has spent the past five years developing Eha alongside her partner, the Singaporean-Estonian entrepreneur Sonny Aswani. “Nothing can be forced.”

For Maran and Aswani, the journey to creating Eha began halfway across the world, during a walk on a wellness retreat in India. After years of splitting their time (and their busy careers) between Singapore and Estonia—at one point, Aswani’s family conglomerate was contributing 1% of the latter’s GDP—whenever the couple had a moment to hit pause and visit one of the world’s top holistic sanctuaries, they found themselves returning to a single question: How do we return to what really matters? And why travel to the ends of the earth to find the kind of serenity that already existed in their own northern European backyard?

The answer led them to this unspoiled corner of Estonia, to build a place where their distinct family histories—Maran’s grandfather was born on Hiiumaa, while Aswani’s great-grandfather was a traditional Sindhi healer—could overlap with their shared reverence for the land, their ancestral roots, and their fascination with the power of holistic healing. “Hiiumaa is not an obvious place for a luxury retreat, and that is exactly why it felt right,” Maran explains. “It has a quietness and authenticity that you cannot really create.” Rather than impose their vision on the landscape, they decided to “listen to it and build something that felt as though it belonged there.”

Think of Hiiumaa as Estonia’s wilder, more windswept version of Martha’s Vineyard: a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with miles of white-sand beaches and moss-carpeted forests, dotted with traditional timber farmhouses and medieval stone churches. While locals typically make the journey via a quick prop-plane hop from Tallinn or a leisurely mainland ferry, the most seamless route for international travelers is actually via Finland: After touching down in Helsinki and spending a night beneath the Belle Époque chandeliers of the freshly restored Hotel Kämp—the city’s storied, 19th-century grand dame—I boarded a private charter with Helsinki Citycopter for a breathtaking, 45-minute flight over the emerald islets of the Baltic Sea.

Hiiumaa moves at a very different pace from the Finnish capital, however. It’s long served as a popular summer getaway for Estonians, and more recently those who have prospered thanks to Tallinn’s tech boom over the past two decades: When I visited in June, families could be spotted hopping onto sailboats in the Kärdla marina, catching the early summer breeze to head out seal-watching, or gathering outside the beachside restaurants for smoked fish and cold beers.

Despite the island’s influx of visitors every summer, building a luxury retreat in such a remote location came with its fair share of challenges—though ultimately, it was a reminder to work with the land rather than against it. “It would have been easy at certain points to add more, to make things bigger, or to follow what the wellness industry is doing elsewhere,” Maran admits. “But we kept returning to the same principle: We wanted Eha to feel grown, not built, and that kind of feeling cannot be rushed.”

To bring that vision to life, they assembled an all-star roster of Estonian creatives: architect Tiit Trummel designed the Main House, while Studio Argus and Vaikla Studio worked on the interior architecture of the main hub and surrounding Forest Houses, employing a calming palette of untreated timber, lime plaster, and muted earth tones that reflect the shifting light of the forest and sea. Landscape architect Kristiina Hellström developed a series of wild coastal meadows, organic kitchen gardens, and wandering forest trails. Virtually every object has been sourced from makers across the country: Guests wrap themselves in custom robes by Tallinn-based fashion designer Katrin Kuldma of Amanjeda, dine off earthy ceramic tableware by Uluala, and wash with organic sea buckthorn and juniper bath products crafted by Hiiumaa-based artisans Hiiuihuhooldus. Even the property’s custom-woven fabrics incorporate coastal stripes and geometric folk motifs, paying homage to the island’s centuries-old wool-weaving traditions.

But the real draw here, of course, is its spectacular setting. There are few spots on the island (or indeed, anywhere in the Baltics) quite as arresting as where Eha has positioned itself along the southeastern coast: an octagonal, thatch-roofed architectural wonder, it hovers above a mirror-like tidal stream on the edge of an ancient pine forest, where blue-black barn swallows (the Estonian national bird) chirp among the reeds. “In Estonia, nature is a religion, and the forest is our church,” says Maran. Even the fiercest skeptic would struggle to disagree that there’s a powerfully elemental, even spiritual charge to the land here.

That ethos informs every layer of the guest experience, which has been curated by general manager and wellness director Amber Gauci-Ward around three pillars: circadian rhythm alignment, nervous system regulation, and a meaningful connection to nature, self, and others. The circadian rhythm aspect is especially intriguing: Each chapel-like suite is outfitted with circadian-aligned lamps to begin the day, while meals are served deliberately early to help you digest before dozing off at 9 p.m. sharp, lulled by a spatial sleep soundscape in the room conceived in partnership with the acoustic studio Olo.

If that sounds a little too regimented on paper, it isn’t in practice. The intention here is to ground you in the simpler things: brisk Baltic walks, or sipping herbal tea in one of the nooks and crannies “for daydreaming,” or lying out on a blanket in one of the fields after the lights have been dimmed, and the night sky becomes dazzlingly bright. “I think the wellness and longevity industries can sometimes overcomplicate things,” Maran notes. “There is so much science and innovation now, which is wonderful, but it can also become overwhelming. At Eha, we are returning to the basics: fresh air, clean water, nourishing food, natural light, minimal light pollution, good sleep, meaningful connection, and time in nature.”

And because Eha’s calendar is dictated by those five distinct Nordic seasons, no two stays look quite the same. A fall retreat focuses on grounding and harvest, with Estonian peat-steam rituals, mushroom foraging, and guided bog trails, while winter embraces deep rest through snowshoeing, dusk lantern walks, and Yoga Nidra by the fireplace. The fleeting weeks of varakevad—or springrise—will see you wake in the mornings to head out for maple sap collection and somatic movement sessions, while the luminous Nordic summers open up to berry harvesting, wild swimming, and botanical cocktails at twilight. (There are plenty of top-tier facial and body rituals on offer, too: some draw on 2,000-year-old therapeutic sea mud harvested from nearby Käina Bay wetland, as well as bioactive bog peat developed by Estonian skincare innovator Aesti; other therapies use international plant-powered lines like Seed to Skin Tuscany and Ground.)

The food, too, moves with the micro-seasons. Firmly rejecting the restrictive nature of traditional spa cuisine, Eha’s organic-forward kitchen—helmed by Green Michelin-starred chef Peeter Pihel—is generously portioned while remaining, like everything else, deeply rooted in the island’s terroir. “We are not trying to make wellness food feel austere—we want it to feel generous, grounding, and deeply satisfying,” says Maran. Meals are augmented by daytime adaptogenic elixirs, functional mushroom tonics from Estonian producer Shroomwell, and hands-on fermentation and culinary workshops. Mushrooms are a seriously big deal here—during my visit, I was invited to drill a hole in the side of a birch tree and plant a chaga mushroom with a small marker beside it, to encourage me to come back and check on its progress on my next visit.

With its distinctive and deeply thoughtful philosophy, one senses there will be a lot of repeat guests arriving for Eha’s three- to seven-night wellness programs, swapping pinging inboxes and calendar alerts for birch saunas and forest bathing. I know that after seeing the grounds in high summer, I was deeply curious to see how they appear in the golden splendor of fall and the moody winter mists. Oh, and the spring, too: It’s then that you can try apitherapy, in which guests are invited to rest among the beehives (fear not: you’ll be protected from any stings within an enclosed relaxation bed) to absorb the healing energy of their vibrations and the scent of propolis. “So much of modern life pulls us away from our own rhythm,” Maran adds. “At Eha, I hope people feel that rhythm slowly returning.”

#6714. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6713. Nina Katchadourian Spent 11 Years Making Art on Airplanes

The hundreds of photographs are gathered in a new book, Seat Assignment

There are few places where the unwieldiness and malleability of time take center stage quite like when one is on an airplane. It is one of the few times when the world allows for a kind of self-indulgence: You can sleep, catch up on your favorite TV shows, watch a guilty pleasure movie, read a book, or listen to a podcast that you never had time for while on the ground, or you could even raw-dog the flight, just you and your thoughts, getting lost as you hurl through the air at 580 miles per hour inside a hunk of aluminum and other composite materials.

In 2010, the artist Nina Katchadourian was sitting on a plane at LaGuardia Airport in New York on her way to Atlanta, begrudging all of the frequent flying that was keeping her away from her studio and her work. “I thought, ‘Here I am again, about to spend three hours flying somewhere, and it feels as if this time already doesn’t count,’ ” she recalls thinking. “It’s garbage time.” But Katchadourian, whose interdisciplinary approach has led her to work with a wide array of mediums and materials (photography, performance, sculpture, “audio interventions,” a popcorn machine), called herself out. “I thought [it was] a really bad attitude for somebody like me, who claims as an artist to be interested in mundane things and everyday things and believes that things often deserve a closer look.” She challenged herself to “make things the whole way to Atlanta” with whatever she could find around her, photographed with her iPhone. The first “improvisations,” as she called them, included classic airplane objets like pretzels (see them resting comfortably on a king bed), straws (turned into bridges over a mountainscape, and the shiny buckle on the seatbelt (a perfect medium for a self-portrait). “By the time I got to Atlanta, I thought, ‘I need to keep doing this because something just happened and I need to see where it will go.’ ” She’d work on it until 2021, when the pandemic provided a natural pause.

Now the entire project has been published as a small tome appropriately titled Seat Assignment. The hundreds of images are a testament to how curiosity about the world can open and create an alternate universe that lives exactly within the limits of our own, and Katchadourian is open to both the humorous (a little puppet face made from a bread roll with blueberries for eyes and a strawberry tongue, politicians and businessmen with noses and beards made out of pieces of croissants and radishes, a pile of sweater that resembles a gorilla) and the sublime (a Stonehenge-esque architectural formation made from mint Life Savers, mountains dotted with sweater-fuzz black clouds, mysterious trees with twisted-napkin vines that wrap around them). On a particularly long flight from San Francisco to Auckland, New Zealand, she holed up in the lavatory and produced a series of portraits “in the Flemish style,” repurposing toilet-seat covers and paper towels into dramatic collars and hats. The portraits are uncanny, often capturing the masters’ chiaroscuro effect.

She quickly set some ground rules as she embarked on the project: She wouldn’t bring anything to “make” art on the plane, could only work with what she found, and would only use her iPhone to document what she’d made. “I felt like doing [those things] would make everything too easy, and it would make it all too much like ‘art,’ ” she explains. Curiously, during the years she worked on Seat Assignment, the quality of the camera on the iPhone improved so much that it being part of her rules became less important. “In those early days, people would say to me, ‘Well, why aren’t you using a real camera?’ ” she explains. “That question disappeared after a while.”

In a way, it seems like it was only a matter of time before Katchadourian embarked on an airplane project. As a child, she traveled every summer with her parents and younger brother from Northern California, where she grew up, to a small island off the south coast of Finland, where her mother’s family was from. The island was hugely influential on how she saw the world (“I’ve made a lot of artwork there, and I really feel like my approaches to artmaking have been learned there”), but so was the long flight itself. She’d make up games with her brother, trying to guess the movie that would play during the flight (back in the day when there was only one television screen for passengers to watch). On one occasion, her mother brought sheets and blankets and made a bed and pillows for the two young children on the floor beneath their seats. “They would never let you do this now, but I remember when it was my turn to sleep down there, looking to the side and seeing this landscape of legs that went through the whole plane. It was amazing, an underworld of under the seats.” She adds, “The whole plane was a place that we were all temporary residents of, and it wasn’t a place I disliked at all. It was this space that took us from one place I loved to another place I loved.”

This point of view has guided much of her work, like “Sorted Books,” another ongoing project she started in 1993, where she organizes book collections—whether belonging to a friend or an institution—into poems or literary fragments; “The Genealogy of the Supermarket,” which began in 2005, where she organizes all of the “people” that feature in grocery products (Betty Crocker, Orville Redenbacher, the Gerber Baby) into a genealogical tree; and “Mended Spiderwebs,” where she completed spiderwebs with delicate red thread. Though disparate, her projects always invite audiences to truly look at the world around them. “I think for the first 10 years it used to concern me a lot that I never did the same things two times in a row,” Katchadourian says. “After a while, I realized that’s actually a methodology. It’s not a deficit; it’s a way of working. A way of saying the medium is secondary to the approach.”

“I think a lot of projects for me have come out of a ‘what if?’ sort of question that I ask myself, and then I try to sort out an inquiry,” she says. Curiosity and happenstance, or the idea of chance, are essential in Katchadourian’s practice. “The weird thing about research is that you don’t always know that you’re doing it, so sometimes you’re reading or having experiences and only later do you realize, ‘Oh, all that curiosity was actually in service of trying to figure this thing out.’ ” She continues, “I think you have to take diversions seriously because they are showing you something back if you’re willing to observe yourself doing it. There’s something in it that often holds a lot of information.” It’s also what her work does.
