On Tuesday evening, all that glitters was indeed gold—and adorned in diamonds. For the third year in a row, Tiffany & Co.’s festive fête at its Fifth Avenue flagship served as the unofficial ribbon-cutting moment to kick off the holiday season, hosted this time around by Amanda Seyfried.

The actress, who is the House’s newest ambassador, was also tapped to illuminate the Bird on a Rock installation. A glitzed-up and glammed-out guest list made its way to Midtown for the occasion, passing the Fifth Avenue snowflake—now lit in Tiffany Blue for the holiday season—and stopping to marvel at the Landmark’s twinkling facade.

A brief elevator ride upstairs opened up to reveal a winter wonderland. Sparkling displays showcased the House’s pieces in front of the floor-to-ceiling windows, trays were laden with Tiffany Blue martinis, and the belle of the ball—the Bird on a Rock—gleamed outside. As guests counted down the moments until its lighting, they nibbled on petite T&C stamped-paninis and micro tuna crispy rice bites.

Seyfried arrived, dazzling in a Tiffany HardWear white gold and pavé diamond link necklace and the hallmark Bird on a Rock Wing brooch—with over 13 carats of diamonds. The award-winning star was just as excited for the party as everyone else. “As a young American girl, you have these fantasies that you might get to be a part of something really special. It’s pretty iconic that I’m here and that I get to represent Tiffany for the holiday season. There’s something very classic, traditional, and symbolic about Tiffany’s—it’s the best legacy jewelry brand there is,” Seyfried told Vogue. “My sister-in-law is here tonight with her baby, my godson. I wish my kids were here, but I didn’t even think to invite them, and they’re actually in the city. I don’t know what I was thinking!”

The holidays evoke all types of fuzzy feelings, and Mikey Madison reminisced about one of her favorite family traditions. “My dad and I always cook, so we’ll cook a big Hanukkah dinner and we’ll do all the classics that my grandma used to make. He does the brisket, I’ll do the latkes, the matzah ball soup, the kugel,” Madison shared. “It’s always meaningful to go to an event with Tiffany. It feels like a big family for me, and there’s so much intention behind their artistry, what they do, and how they bring people together,” the Oscar-winning ambassador added. “It’s the loveliest job that I have to get to work with them and get to wear all this incredibly beautiful jewelry as well.”

When it was finally time to light the Bird on a Rock, everyone gathered near the tree—one constructed from countless coveted Blue Boxes. “Love is a gift,” Matthieu Garnier, president and CEO of Tiffany & Co. North America, told the crowd during his toast. “The most meaningful gifts carry stories, create memories, and connect generations.”

Garnier wasn’t just referring to the tree: The entire 2026 holiday campaign—starring Seyfried—centers on gifts becoming future heirlooms, which in turn bridge a connection between generations. Just like in 1965, when Jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock design became one of those treasured keepsakes intended to be passed down.

Right on cue, Seyfried stepped up, placing a Tiffany ornament on the tree, and immediately, the Bird on a Rock shimmered to life, illuminating the bustling streets below. Let the holidays begin!

#6670. I Stood on a Vibration Plate Every Day for Two Weeks. I Have Thoughts.

Why is everyone suddenly raving about this vibrating plate for lymphatic drainage, muscle recovery, and more?

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

When it comes to personality types, I consider myself part of a unique subset: Type A minus. This means I am Type A most of the time, like when I’m traveling, and because my calendar and to-do list are my lifelines. Still, I lean more toward Type B when it comes to my unread text messages or how many times I snooze my alarm (hint: Both are high numbers). But one thing I am most certainly extra Type A about is my wellness routine.

I recently created a shared note on my iPhone with my friend that lists every supplement or health powder I take, when I take it, and links to the products. But my newest wellness obsession has nothing to do with an ingestible boost—it’s a device that may transport you back to an ’80s workout video à la Olivia Newton-John.

Vibration plates are all over my TikTok algorithm, but athletes widely used them in the ’70s and ’80s to improve performance and recovery. “They were first used in rehab and even in astronaut training to help prevent muscle and bone loss, but now they’ve become popular in gyms and at home for general fitness and wellness,” says Jeff Paul, the director of personal training at Chelsea Piers Fitness.

Today, it seems like everyone on my For You page has incorporated the vibrating plate into their routine, so I decided to see what all the chatter was about for myself. “Vibration plates gently vibrate while you stand, sit, or exercise on them. Those small, rapid vibrations make your muscles contract many times per second—way more than they would during a normal workout,” adds Paul. “When used correctly, vibration plates can help improve circulation and lymphatic flow, which supports recovery and reduces fluid buildup.”

It seems simple: a vibrating plate, but when you stand on the jiggling, high-motion platform (though speed settings are adjustable), your muscles are gently activated to promote lymphatic flow, aid workout recovery, and increase blood circulation. These plates claim to activate hundreds of muscles (even those your regular Pilates or cycling class can’t target), which may help slightly increase muscle mass. They also claim to increase bone density, helping to prevent osteoporosis, a condition that often occurs naturally as we age.

“Research supports vibration plates [are beneficial] for muscle strengthening, improved bone density, and reduced risk of falls," says Sarah Koehl, doctor of physical therapy at WAVE Physical Therapy & Pilates. "They can be particularly helpful for older adults or for anyone who cannot perform traditional strength training at higher loads.”

When shopping for vibration plates, I came across several categories—the two most popular being linear and oscillating, which move from side to side and tend to be gentler on joints. I opted for the latter option from LifePro. However, if you want to bulk up, Koehl adds that vibration plates provide slightly more—if not the same—muscle-mass increase as regular strength training, and a vertical plate is better for building muscle.

Vibration plates have a slew of versatile benefits. They can also be used for lymphatic drainage, which is what motivated me to adopt the device. Alternatively, you can work out on the plate, adding it to a push-up or squat routine to intensify the exercise. Using the device is pretty simple: I stand on the plate for 10 minutes a day and let the vibrations do the work. When I first started using the LifePro Vibra device, I used speed setting 2, but I’ve worked my way up to 6. What I love about the LifePro Vibra is that it is voice-controlled and comes with a remote, so I can change the speed and treatment time with my voice or a touch—without getting off the plate mid-session.

Paul urges you not to overuse a vibrating plate. “Too high a setting or too long a session can cause joint discomfort or dizziness,” he explains. “If you have a pacemaker, recent surgery, or any medical condition, definitely check with your doctor first. Otherwise, start slow and see how your body responds.”

I consistently used the LifePro Vibra for 10 minutes every morning, usually after a workout, to aid in recovery and reduce morning bloat. I’ve heard stories of people who experienced immediate bowel movements or reduced bloating after using the device. While my results haven’t been that dramatic, I’ve definitely noticed a difference since I started using it. First, my muscles feel less sore, even after trying new workouts that target different muscle groups than usual. I also love using the plate as an extra layer of lymphatic drainage because the movement kick-starts my lymphatic system and helps avoid stagnant fluid, even on days when I don’t work out.

"Vibration plates are not a magic solution," Paul says. "You’ll get the most out of them when you pair the vibration with movement. So instead of just standing on it, try squats, lunges, or balance work. That’s when you’ll see real improvements in muscle engagement, circulation, and stability. On their own, they’re more of a supplement to your training than a replacement for it."

One thing to note: the device is bulky, especially in a small New York City apartment like mine. However, it can easily slide under a bed or behind a dresser. Whether you want to channel an ’80s fitness routine or improve lymphatic drainage, vibration plates are definitely worth trying if you have the space.

#6669. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6668. Why This 251-Year-Old Watchmaker Is Suddenly Hotter Than Ever in 2026

Welcome to GQ’s 201-level Watch Glossary, breaking down the brands, advanced terms, and specific references that are essential knowledge for every serious collector.

Founded in the late 18th century by perhaps the world’s most famous watchmaker, Abraham Louis-Breguet, the eponymous brand was once the horologer to royalty. (He famously made a watch for Marie Antoinette that she unfortunately, ahem, never got the chance to wear.) Breguet is responsible for the tourbillon, an early self-winding mechanism, his famous namesake numerals that nearly every brand in Switzerland uses now, and much more. But despite its massive contributions to horology, the brand's pieces haven't caused frenzies among collectors like those from Rolex, Patek Philippe, or even Cartier. However, like Dune’s Bene Gesserit, the watchmaker’s plans are apparently measured in centuries. Recent signals point to the idea that Breguet may be entering a new golden era as collectors come around to its exquisitely made timepieces.

Follow the money, and you’ll quickly find evidence of Breguet’s glow-up. Late last month, at Monaco Legends Group’s fall watch auction, a 1970s-era piece previously owned by a 50-year veteran Breguet watchmaker sold for €221,000. That was nearly of the beginning of the brand's impressive run of auction that makes us wonder, What’s going on with Breguet these days?

Abraham Louis-Breguet isn’t the only hallowed watchmaker to steer the brand. Legendary names like George Daniels, F.P. Journe, and Michel Parmigiani have contributed to the brand’s legacy. At auction, many collectors are keying in on a period of Breguet led by Daniel Roth from the mid-’70s to 1987. After he left Breguet, Roth went on to found his own successful brand that now sells for six figures at auction. The combination of these two powers is proving irresistible to today’s collectors.

The Ref. 3050A was a signature piece of Roth’s reign at Breguet and epitomizes the designer’s contributions to the brand. Roth introduced the first modern piece from the manufacturer with a perpetual calendar. The piece’s guilloché dial is also a signature of the Roth era. The watch sold for €85,800 at the end of October.

The 3057 was the successor to Roth’s first watch at Breguet, the 3050. The big change is the transparent caseback. This lovely semi-skeletonized perpetual calendar hammered for some 200% above its estimate—not a huge surprise considering Breguet made only a couple of these a year when they were in production. Notably, thanks to the addition of that exhibition caseback, we can see the pretty, highly decorated automatic movement.

It’s platinum. It’s skeletonized. It’s got a tourbillon. It’s got a matching bracelet. It’s accompanied by all its factory goodies. What else could one ask for in a pre-owned Breguet? Still, a $387,000 hammer price is a remarkable outcome.

Classique Grandes Complications ref. 5447

This oversized perpetual-calendar minute repeater, likewise executed in platinum, commanded almost $271,000 at Phillips this weekend—proof positive of the appeal of classical Breguet looks mixed with modern movement technology and finishing.

An evolution of the Daniel Roth-era ref. 3350, this gorgeous tourbillon wristwatch features one of the hallmarks of Breguet’s signature style: a beautifully guilloché dial combined with blued steel hands and a Roman-numeral minute track.

Breguet took a significant left turn in the 1950s when it began producing the Type XX flyback chronograph for French military aviators. It still serves as an important pillar in the brand’s lineup today.

Introduced in the late 1980s, the ref. 3350 is Breguet’s first wrist-worn tourbillon—a significant milestone for the brand that invented the complication. Emblematic of the Daniel Roth era of Breguet production, it has since become a neo-vintage classic.

Released in 2025 in celebration of the firm’s 250th birthday, the Classique Souscription uses a single hand to tell the time against a Grand Feu enamel dial mirroring vintage Breguet pocket watches. Just this week, the maison followed it up with the platinum version seen above.

The Expérimentale 1 is the first step in a new collection of envelope-pushing, ultra-complicated watches. Fitted with advanced materials, the “1” features watchmaking’s very first high-frequency tourbillon, which beats at an astounding 10 Hz. This is a great way forward for modern Breguet—a model that embraces the brand’s tradition as the industry's most inventive watchmaker.

Now a quarter-millennium old, Breguet has one of the most extensive histories of any watchmaker still in operation, with records reaching back generations. Its finishing is exceptional; its complications are rooted in some of the earliest experiments by one of the world’s most famous horologists; and its designs are superb. As prices continue to skyrocket for watches at auction, especially for hotshot newcomers, it’s exciting to see one of the most storied brands in history catch fire, too.

#6667. Madewell and The Six Bells Bring Storybook Charm to the Holidays

The Hudson Valley inn lends its old-world touch to the brand.

There’s nothing quite like the holiday season to boost your sense of nostalgia for cozy moments at home—especially when they involve a touch of cold-weather whimsy. Whether you’re sipping on a hot coffee or tea as you watch the changing leaves or you’re curled up next to a warm fireplace with your latest read, the colder months of the year are primed for ample charm. Of course, these moments are not without their accoutrements, which is right where the new Madewell collaboration with The Six Bells—a country inn located in the Hudson Valley—comes in.

The Six Bells Inn, founded by Audrey Gelman, features interiors inspired by the imagined English village known as Barrow’s Green—complete with its own fictional characters and landmarks—giving the space an old-world touch that feels as if it’s been plucked right out of a storybook. It’s this distinct aesthetic, along with Gelman’s way of storytelling, that led to the inn’s collaboration with Madewell.

“Steven [Cateron, Madewell’s creative director,] and the team at Madewell understood our little world at Six Bells from the very first conversation we had. In the early stages of working together on this collaboration, we wanted this collection to feel like stepping through a doorway into another time where things feel a little more enchanted,” Gelman told ELLE.com in an email. “Every piece in the collection was designed to have that sense of wonder. We hope it brings the spirit of The Six Bells into people’s lives and homes this holiday season.”

With a range of apparel, accessories, and home décor—including vintage-inspired needlepoint ornaments and pillows, stockings, and toiletry bags featuring custom prints based on the inn’s interiors—the collection combines Madewell’s laid-back style with The Six Bells’s country charm. “For the first time, we’re really leaning into home accents, which let us extend [the Madewell] world beyond what you wear and into the spaces you live in,” Cateron said in an email. “The inn’s wallpapers and patterns were a huge source of inspiration, and you’ll find bits of them throughout the collection, right down to the lining of our Denim Trucker Jacket.” There are also pajama sets and even a nightgown for those who want to take one of summer’s biggest trends straight into the holiday season. And with prices ranging from $17 to $248, there are plenty of pieces ready for the gift-giving season (and no doubt, whoever receives these will be tickled to unwrap them).

#6666. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and Wardrobe.NYC Feted Their Next Collaboration at Chateau Marmont

Los Angeles may slow down on Sunday evenings, but this past weekend, Chateau Marmont was anything but quiet. On the patio of the hotel’s penthouse, Wardrobe.NYC hosted an al fresco dinner celebrating its latest collaboration with supermodel Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, who also serves as fashion director at FWRD, where the 15-piece collection is exclusively available to shop.

Despite the gusty weather—which left half the table in near darkness as candles repeatedly blew out—longtime fans of the brand turned out for the occasion, including Laura Harrier, Lauren Perez, Vittoria Ceretti, Kirsty Godso, and Stephanie Suganami.

Not only was the first installment of the ongoing collaboration—a lineup of sculptural black-and-white separates that launched in 2024—a smashing success, but it also sparked a close bond between the brand and the style maven. “After the first one, we didn’t want it to be over,” Christine Centenera, a stylist and Vogue Australia’s editor-in-chief who co-founded the line with designer Josh Goot, told Vogue. Centenera was similarly effusive about Huntington-Whiteley’s magnetic energy and work ethic. “She’s really funny and can take criticism well, and she always has a creative solution,” Centenera noted.

The team took cues from the first drop when designing the second installment. “One of the top-selling pieces from the original line was a sculpted blazer, and so that kind of architectural feel was brought through into this collection,” Huntington-Whiteley, in a shearling stole from the capsule, explained. She then turned her attention to Ceretti, who was hobnobbing near the bar. “Vittoria is wearing the really cool shrunken leather bomber and great leather trousers [from the collection],” she added.

Huntington-Whiteley was equally grateful for the trio’s growing friendship. “I get to spend time with two incredibly talented people in the industry, two of my close friends, and create my dream collection that I want to fill my own wardrobe with,” she said. Ultimately, Huntington-Whiteley wanted to develop a versatile lineup that she could mix and match during her hectic international schedule. “It was all about creating a collection that I can keep in my suitcase and travel around with,” she shared. “It’s about the idea of a little black dress and those staple pieces that can take you from trips to events.”

For the first hour of the evening, guests mingled over cocktails and wine, taking in the twinkling city skyline. “The view here is magic,” said entrepreneur Perez, who arrived in a cropped blazer and slouchy low-rise trousers from the label.

Meanwhile, Raissa Gerona, Revolve’s president of brand and partnerships, looked around the lively crowd, appreciative of the community that had come together for the occasion. “Everybody’s so busy, people have kids, and it’s a Sunday, so people have work tomorrow,” she said. “So for everyone to show up to support Rosie and the brand, that’s the best thing I can ask for.”

Attendees settled into their seats at a candlelit table on the terrace, where servers promptly arrived with baguettes and French butter, roasted beet salad with goat cheese, burrata and tomatoes, and yellowtail crudo. Centenera and Huntington-Whiteley then rose to address the intimate crowd, thanking everyone—as much as possible over the whistling wind—for coming out to celebrate their latest creative pursuit.

Once guests finished their first round of dishes, the main course arrived: roasted chicken with mixed vegetables, and prime petit filet with asparagus spears, grilled broccolini, and truffle fries. The night ended on a sweet note, with bowls of berries and cream served for dessert, banishing any sign of the Sunday scaries.

#6664. Why Blake Griffin Couldn’t Leave Basketball Alone

Twelve years ago, I was sitting in Blake Griffin’s house, listening to him tell me that under no circumstances would he stay around basketball after he retired. “Well, look who’s a liar,” he says now.

Griffin is a former NBA All-Star who played for 14 years, many of them for the Clippers, before announcing his retirement in 2024. He now has his own show, The Stepback with Blake Griffin, and a weekly gig with NBA on Prime, as part of their studio show. “I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players,” Griffin says. “This is a job that 400-something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t.”

On The Stepback, Griffin puts on a suit, sits behind a desk, and addresses a big, sports-related topic each week: the media, taxpayer-financed stadiums, the rocketing costs of youth sports, and so on. Like him, the show is unexpectedly funny, frequently insightful, and a good hang. In this conversation, he and I discuss the Clippers then and now, retiring at 34, and what it was like to have some rude journalist visit his house, all those years ago.

The following conversation is lightly edited and condensed from the latest episode of One More Question with Zach Baron. Watch below or on YouTube. Listen on Spotify or Apple Podcasts.

Blake Griffin: It’s funny, being 37 now, looking back at that time, and being like: “Man, I didn’t know what I was doing.” I can’t believe people were entrusting me with having a house and a car and doing all these adult things. I wasn’t an adult yet.

Well, in fairness to me, I’d only been living there for four years—no, I think it was fairly new at the time. I moved into that house at the end of 2013 and we spoke the next year. So over time you collect more stuff, figure out your taste.

He walked me through the entire party for—it felt like an hour, I don’t know, I had lost track of time. When you’re holding a 70-something-year-old man’s hand who’s not related to you, being introduced to party guests—and I think I was 19 at the time, I’d just gotten drafted—time sort of slows down. So I don’t know how long it was. Could have been half a day. But yeah, from the first time I met him, it was a very different experience.

Everybody, when I first moved there, was like, “Where are you from?” I’m like, “From Oklahoma.” And they’re like, “Oh, so—horses?” I’m like, “Well, yeah, but also cars.” It’s a civilized place. Culture shock in just that—I didn’t live in Hollywood, but you’re just in LA and that’s the epicenter of so much. It was a lot, but also you’re so focused when you’re 19. Apartment, practice facility, airport—those are the three things that I did. So it kind of gave me time to grow up. And then when we met, I was a much more seasoned man at 24, 25. It’s crazy looking back, because you’re like, “Man, I can’t believe I moved there at 19.” I tell people all the time, I grew up in LA.

I didn’t really dwell on that question. I don’t know. It was cool. I really enjoyed our conversation.

No, it’s fine. I was going there on my own. It’s fine. I’m happy to give one. I did. I enjoyed our conversation. I was actually thinking about it on the way here. Those are the best conversations—when you can just sit and talk and there’s not just these six questions that you’ve got to hit. You just let the conversation go where it goes. That’s what the conversation felt like to me.

Well, look who’s a liar. You know what’s crazy is, I never envisioned myself doing the NBA on Prime Show. And even until I retired and had conversations about going to join TNT or ESPN, whatever it was, and I still didn’t want to. And it really was Amazon getting a part of the TV rights and them really wanting to do a show differently than what was already on air. And that intrigued me because I thought there was this space in the NBA particularly where you can just analyze games, you can talk about basketball. And I always thought that there was a little bit too much negativity when it came to scrutinizing players. This is a job that 400 something guys have. It’s extremely hard. I don’t need to go on TV and I don’t need to tell everybody that the guy that went three for 17 sucks at basketball. He doesn’t. He had an off night. Instead, maybe I can walk you through some of the things he maybe could have done differently or some of the things he did well and it just wasn’t his night.

It’s kind of how I talk just in real life. I don’t want to harp on somebody who’s going through a shooting slump. Trust me, no one in the world wants to shoot better than the guy who’s in a shooting slump. It happened to me. Trust me. So I don’t need to come on TV and talk about it. So it’s kind of the same way I talk to people just in real life about certain games or what happened with this, what happened with that? It doesn’t always have to be negative.

I still do. I think that the day that I am bitter, or the day that I watch the game and I only see it from a negative standpoint or I’m like, “Back in our day, we didn’t do this or these guys are getting paid too much money”—I think that’s probably the day that I don’t need to do this anymore, because if I’m not going to adapt to where the game is today, I think that’s where you end up being jaded and you end up being biased in your observation or your analysis. And that’s what we’re hired to do, give our analysis. But it’s also like: Give your analysis on basketball today. It doesn’t matter what happened back then. And so my biggest thing too is every year I try to spend time with coaches, GMs, whoever it is, to keep understanding where the game is going, because it does change. Basketball evolves and you have to evolve your mindset around it.

We’re actually boys now. We went and did this golf thing together. I can’t lie. I was always just like, “What? Why? Give me a break, man.” I never was like, “Gosh, Charles is awesome.” Then you spend time with him and you see who he is and I appreciate it. I wasn’t the only person and at times it’s also not unwarranted. There’s games I played bad, I could have done better and this and that. And if that’s his style and that’s how he does it, that’s totally fine. It’s not that you can’t be critical. I just think I wanted to do [it] a little different.

There are definitely guys like that. My advice, if you’re in that spot, or something I wish somebody had told me when I was in this transition of really trying to develop my game, but also I was known for being aggressive, athletic, attack the rim, is you can continue to develop this skill and you continue to work on your game, but don’t go away from the things that got you to this place in the first place. So I would say to guys, use your athleticism, get to the rim, put pressure on the rim and then let that be your play making because now people have to rotate over, they have to help. Now you can open up different parts of your game. So a lot of times players hear all this like, “He can’t do this, he can’t do that.” And sometimes you kind of block out what you do well and you’re just so focused on what people are saying you can’t do.

Yeah. I mean, it’s almost impossible not to. I wouldn’t read tweets. I don’t read mentions during the season especially, but I wouldn’t put a lot of thought into comments, but it’s hard not to... When you’re just watching sports and you love watching sports and there’s morning shows on and it’s all around you, you’re going to hear stuff. And then there’s also the side of you that you know what you need to get better at as well.

I watched the game a little bit differently. I think as a player, I was watching so much of player tendencies, like I’m going to be guarding this guy in a couple days, or whatever it is. You’re also watching plays, you’re seeing teams run different sets. And now I’m interested a little bit more in the chess match that’s happening because trying to analyze, you’re looking at, okay, “What are the matchups? What would I have maybe done differently in that matchup? What could they do differently? What worked well? What didn’t work well?” And then you’re watching both sides of the ball, obviously. So it’s a lot of the same obviously basketball viewing, but I think when you’re trying to watch from an analyst perspective, you have to be a little bit more all-encompassing. When I’m watching as a player at night, if we don’t have a game, I’m not really tuning into, “Oh, since so-and-so got a tech, they’ve been on a 7-0 run,” but that’s something you clock now because it’s part of telling the story of the game.

I think it was my time. I think when I got to the point where I still enjoyed the game of basketball, but I was enjoying less and less everything else that came with it. My last several years I was in Detroit, I was in Brooklyn, I was in Boston, and my kids are in school in Los Angeles. So being away from them was tough. Even getting to see them once a month is still a little bit brutal. Or you’re on the road, you come back here, you get a couple days. So that wore on me. I also had an unfortunate amount of injuries, and I felt like I was having to put just as much in just to practice and then recover from that practice and then get ready for the game the next day, and it became this whole thing. I felt like I wanted to walk away from basketball on my own terms. I had a chance to go play another year and took some time to think about it, and I just felt like it was my time.

I don’t think there was a specific moment. I did remember when training camp came back around that next season and I was still trying to decide and I realized I didn’t feel like I was missing anything. I was like, “Oh, all right. Not as scary as I thought it would be.” Then as the season went on, I just didn’t see myself going back. I remember I was playing golf with JJ Redick once before I retired. This was before he took the job with the Lakers, and he said something to me that just stuck with me. He was like, “I’m telling you, you won’t be truly happy until you retire.” It kind of shocked me. Because he and I played together for five years, I think, and we were so similar in the way we prepared and the way we worked and how much we cared about the game that it just is this all-encompassing, obsessive thing. And it’s hard to really appreciate the little things, and it’s hard to appreciate making your own schedule. The school drop-offs, first day of school, doing all these different things. That’s sort of the way I took it, and the way I think that he meant it—is it’s such a grind, mental grind, physical grind, of putting literally everything you have into this thing. And then when you’re done, you just find this new sense of peace.

It’s amazing. I mean, I hope that they understood why I was having to be gone so much, but just being present is such a huge, huge gift. I mean, literally yesterday, my son had a football game that was two hours outside of LA. I drove two hours to watch an hour and a half football game, and then two hours back, and I was so happy. Now their games are what brings me sports joy.

It’s definitely scary because it’s also the one thing that you’ve done your whole life. And you also have to think—I dropped out of college. A lot of guys don’t even go, or guys are maybe there one year, and you don’t get the college experience of the workload and classes and graduating, internships, your first foray into the working world and you’re learning all these lessons and figuring out who you’re going to be, who you want to be, or how to operate in that world, and you miss out on that, and then you retire. I think a lot of guys have that What now? thing. And for me personally, doing nothing was never an option. I would be bored out of my mind. So that’s one thing I always preach to younger guys is find something you think you may want to do before you’re done.

Even in the offseason, you have to work out. So it’s still all based around this one thing. So even your free time is not quite necessarily like, “Okay, all right, go do whatever you want.” And then the season is so structured and you don’t really think about it. Every move is planned. You have your schedule in advance so you know it. It’s not like a surprise, but there’s no free time. I remember when I got traded to the Pistons, somebody asked me: “So, do you just commute? Are you still living in LA?” And I’m like, “No, no. We play every other day. There’s no commute time.”

You definitely have those moments. I kind of made this thing where whenever you get injured—unfortunately I had several times to perfect this—but I would give myself 24 hours to be upset, mad, angry, whatever, feel sorry for yourself. And then after that, you just have to put everything you have into coming back. But there was a specific one. I tore a ligament on the bottom of my foot in the playoffs in 2017. And I remember that season, I had a chef to make sure all my meals were exactly what I needed. I took my pregame naps in a hyperbaric chamber. I would nap in a hyperbaric chamber on off days, ice baths, hot tub, hot, cold, sauna. I was doing everything possible. And I remember the doctor coming in telling me that I tore my tendon, I had to have surgery, and I just broke down. And that was really the first time I really had a break. The other times it’s a shitty feeling, but I broke down, emotionally broke down. I just remember thinking, “Why me?” And I don’t know. I think I just allowed myself to have that moment, and then you have to just flip the switch and go into surgery and go into rehab and go into that whole process of coming back to the court with everything. Everything you would put into preparing for games, you have to put into that. You have to find a way. And for the most part, I feel like coming back from injuries, I did a pretty solid job. It was kind of like the last one. I felt like: I can’t get back to that certain level.

It’s a weird negotiation you’re having with your body like, “Come on, we’ve always done this. Let’s do it.” It actually is funny because you’re like, “Come on, him? He can’t stop you. Let’s go.” And your body’s just like, “Relax. I’ll tell you what we can do.” But I mean, you know it’s coming. Everybody—I mean, LeBron, I don’t even want to talk about, he’s a freak, guy’s a freak—but you know it’s coming and you just have to make that transition as graceful as possible. I feel like as I got older and when I got to that point, it’s like, Okay, you have more time to put more of yourself into your teammates, into making sure everybody else is good. And it sounds like you’re doing this selfless thing, but that’s part of how you contribute and come to terms with it. There’s different ways to be a team player.

I don’t know. It’s hard to answer that question. I think the thing that I am happy with is I know I worked as hard as I possibly could. To use a sports analogy, I left it all out there on the floor. When I was able to walk away, that’s part of the reason—because like I told you, I was doing everything possible. So when you feel like you laid it all out there and you gave it your true best shot, I think it was easier for me to walk away than to be at the end of my career and be like, “Yeah, but what if I had done this or what if I had done that?”

I mean, there’s definitely things where I’m just like, “I wish I had known this or I wish I had known that.” Earlier in my career, I remember Chris Paul always talking to me about screening angles and this and that. He’s talking about the strategy of how he wants to screen, or what I should be doing. It’s not that I was hearing that and being like, “No, no, I know how to do it.” It was like, you couldn’t quite grasp it until you get it. And as an older player, you start to understand these things better and they become second nature. So you’re not having to think through everything. And so now I’ll see an older clip or an older game and I’m like, “My screen should have been…” Stuff like that where it’s like, “Man, I wish I could go back and tell my younger self.” But then it’s also part of that thing where sometimes you have to experience and you have to understand it on your own. You can tell somebody how to do it, but until it clicks, it doesn’t work.

I miss games, especially the end of the fourth quarter of a close game when I’m watching. I’m like, “Oh man, that looks fun.” But then I’ll get a FaceTime from a buddy who’s still playing and he’s in three degree weather in Chicago on Tuesday in January and he’s going to shootaround and you’re like, “Oof, I don’t know if I miss that part.” So there’s the perspective. Like I said, the games were just the best. They’re the best. And then as I got older, some of the things that came along with it, I think that’s what I wasn’t really prepared for. When I wasn’t excited to do that for a full season, I think that’s when I knew it was time to step away.

I had the idea for this show a long time ago. I was watching John Oliver in 2016, and John Oliver’s the way I make sense of real world issues, politics, whatever’s going on. And it also keeps me entertained and locked in with the comedy aspect. And also always watching these reactionary debate shows, morning TV and basketball or sports in general, and realizing that there’s sort of a void in sports entertainment where it feels like you’re learning about some of these bigger issues that affect fans, sports fans, athletes, and even honestly not fans. I think one of my favorite things was talking to somebody this week who was not really a sports fan. They were like, “Hey, that episode is really cool. I didn’t even think about any of that.” We have a research room, we have a writer’s room, and we’re making sure that I’m not just spewing my personal thoughts or feelings about certain topics, but doing the research and saying, “Hey, I played sports and some of this stuff is still confusing to me, so let me do the research. I will present it to you and you can form your own opinion.” I thought there was a void for that.

I mean, there’s tons of podcasts. There’s so many athlete podcasts and they’re great. I am a listener of some, but like I said, I wanted this to be scripted in the way that you can trust that this is researched information and not just me being like, “Today, on The Blake Griffin Podcast, I’m going to talk about sports journalism. You know what? I got a bone to pick with Stephen A. Smith,” and just going at it from just my perspective.

I mean, one of the best parts about making this show is I felt like I got to utilize a research team to learn about all these topics because the idea of the show isn’t like, “Hey, I played sports. I know what I’m talking about.” It’s, “I played sports, I still don’t really know some of these things.” So being able to try to make sense of that from my perspective was the idea. But man, even just taking a step back to look at analytics and it’s like, “All right, when did this start?” And that’s sort of the entry point to that episode is like, “All right, this is how it started. This is what it’s become, and this is what I think is maybe the issue with it, and this is how we can move forward.” We tried to make every episode not just this like, “Hey, here’s an issue, this sucks.”

The “debate over everything” show was definitely something I was aware of. We were sitting in the training room one time and First Take was on, and it was like Stephen A. Smith and Skip screaming at each other, and the topic was our team, and guys are dying laughing because they’re both just dead wrong. It’s not like one guy you’re like, “Oh, he’s got a good point there.” You’re like, “What are they talking about?” And that was the other thing that sparked my idea for the show was there needs to be something where you can feel like you can rely on what’s being said.

I haven’t heard from him. Here’s my pushback on that. I’m hard on specific things that he said. I’m giving you a very real example, something that actually happened and then talking about it—that to me is a little bit different.

That’s a sports media story. So many guys have found out through Twitter what is going to happen to them in their career. I just wish that I had known and then there was just an upfront conversation like, “Hey, this is what we’re doing.” I remember after the trade, I remember my agent telling me, he was like, “I got calls from several GMs being like, ‘Why didn’t you tell us we would’ve…’” And it maybe was a situation closer to home. So it was like 15, 20 minutes later, the shirt was already out there and people were dying. And then I was like, “Oh my gosh, that is nuts.” I didn’t even clock it in real time.

Yeah. And I’ve since talked to Lawrence Frank, and that was even something he expressed to me too, and zero hard feelings.

Yeah, [I] was definitely bummed about that too. I mean, knowing that was his last year and him going back to the Clippers—that’s a thing that a lot of guys do. It’s like, “I want to finish my career in a place that means a lot to me.” That was tough to see.

It’s been great. We have had a lot of conversations recently, and I think we all look back on that time of—Clippers in general, but that time in general also has a spot in our heart. We had a great time. Unfortunately, we didn’t win a championship. But I think we definitely have a sense of pride.

I definitely look back with a sense of pride. I think with the organization, when I got drafted to the Clippers, they were owned by Donald Sterling, who we touched on—historically bad franchise, it was a punchline. And over the course of eight years of being there, we got Chris Paul, we got JJ, we got all these guys, and we were making runs at not only just getting to the playoffs, but certain years I felt like we had a legitimate chance to win a championship. And obviously we ultimately came short, but I look back on it with a sense of pride more than anything, of trying to leave a place better than you found it. And they continued that success even after we left, and it was always a thing where you look back and you’re like, “It’s cool that we were sort of a team that ushered in that era of not being necessarily a punchline.”

I think I had answered a question that was asked of me and I wasn’t like, “It’s crazy they haven’t done…” It was just kind of like, “We haven’t gone back.” But it’s not a thing. I don’t take the stance of we deserve our time or our time to—it’s not really that. Like I said, if we had won a championship and there was never any recognition of that, sure. I mean, maybe you could be hurt about that, but yeah, that wasn’t a statement of like, “I can’t believe they haven’t had it.” That’s not how I feel at all.

No, I’ll carry the flag, man. I’ll carry the flag. I mean, I’ve said it time and again, Clippers fans here are an incredibly loyal bunch. I don’t think anybody can argue that. They’ve been through a lot of ups and downs, and I love it when I’m out in LA and a Clippers fan comes up to me like, “Hey man, I had Lob City tickets” or “I used to watch you play.” It always means something to me. It’s special. So I don’t shy away from being known as a Clippers player at all.

It’s obviously an unfortunate event. I feel bad for the guys that were in the trade coming to the Clippers. Or not necessarily bad, but if you’re a guy who’s 30, 31—Brandon Ingram, for example, he’s 29 and has been to several different places, a great player still, and now you’re coming to a place that doesn’t have draft picks for the next five years. And it’s not to say he can’t go anywhere else after his contract, but it feels like they were penalized and now those guys just kind of had no say and they’re just on that team and they’re like, “But I didn’t do anything.” And then also the fans, just having to sit through the next five years. And it’s not to say they can’t be competitive. I think they will be competitive. They have a great coach and they have solid pieces on their roster, but it’s hard to move forward as a franchise if you’ve been stripped of five picks. As far as: Did the punishment fit the crime? It’s not really even for me to say, to be honest.

Not really. I think teams will introduce a player’s agent to a company, but then the whole thing is—in an endorsement deal, who’s to say what you’re worth, in my opinion? If Aspiration wants to pay Kawhi, whatever it is, that’s on the company. But now if you’re not doing anything for it, huge red flag. I feel like if you had just planted one tree, just one tree—a bush, have a bonsai tree in your house, anything, I feel like that’s where you could just be like, “All right. I guess that’s what they wanted to pay.” So I think that sure, teams do introduce players to brands, but if you’re doing an endorsement deal and you are doing something for it, shooting a commercial, photo shoot, autograph signing, whatever it is, you can’t really argue.

No, I’ve never heard of a player in my time in the league that was just getting paid by this company to not do anything. Never have.

I prefer the basketball, but I think that’s part of it. I mean, there’s always a story. There’s always something going on. And especially now with players being their own brands and having such huge followings on social media, little tiny things can just become their own thing and it’ll grow on its own. I think it’s part of why basketball is so culturally relevant, but I prefer just the basketball part.

It’s funny because earlier you said, “You could have gone the podcast route and you did it the hard way.” And on top of that, I’m like, “Let’s do late night, that thing that’s definitely dying right now.” So, double down on the hardness of it. But I don’t think you’ve seen these shows go away because they’re just a dead format. I think that some of these shows, it’s budget and expense. Like this show, for example, the budget is not huge at all. I mean, I don’t even know what a regular late night budget is, but I would bet a 50th of that. So figuring out ways to do that format, do the late night format, include sports in today’s world. And thankfully YouTube allows people to do that. It’s one of the best things about it, is creators get to just create what they want. If you can figure out a way to take that format, the old school format and make it work in today’s world, today’s budget, I think that’s how you get things to work.

“Is it hard to date?” I’m married now. Not hard at all, actually. It’s been pretty chill.

Well, for one, for budget reasons, for other reasons, we had to block shoot these. So I shot 14 episodes and we had to keep things pretty evergreen and make sure that we weren’t dating ourselves. So eventually I’d love to get that shooting window from shoot to air much closer. I think season two will accomplish that, but eventually I’d love it to be more of a weekly style show where it’s still broader topics, well researched, scripted, but we’re able to have multiple episodes going at one time. And then if we need to activate one, we can and be able to have a much closer to Last Week Tonight, that format. So it’s truly up to date. I really enjoyed doing this. It was so much fun. As hard as it was and as much work as it was, I had a blast. It’s something that I truly, truly enjoyed. So as long as that joy’s there, I’d love to do it till the wheels fall off.

#6662. Every Outfit TV Is the Digital-Age Fashion Police We Never Knew We Needed

The founders of @everyoutfitonSATC spill the tea on their latest venture into video podcasting

“There are some things that need to be seen to be believed,” says Lauren Garroni, the brunette half of @EveryOutfitonSATC—a Sex and the City fashion archive Instagram account turned Fashion Police-style podcast that she runs with her blonde counterpart, Chelsea Fairless. She’s talking about a stretched canvas image of Dave Navarro walking in the Anna Sui Spring-Summer 1997 runway show, which is currently being sold online by a well-known publishing company. But she might as well have been speaking about the pair’s latest venture: Every Outfit TV.

“Every Outfit is a weekly rundown of the comings and goings in pop culture and fashion,” explains Garroni. She and Fairless launched their podcast in 2021, around the time that the SATC spinoff And Just Like That was announced. Devotees will recall that it was actually phase two, phase one being an Instagram account born in 2016 from Fairless’s frustration with the lack of variety when it came to photos of SATC outfits on the internet. Ten years later, the podcast is viral, the Instagram has 709k followers, and the overall project has morphed into Every Outfit TV, a video component available exclusively on Patreon.

The video format offers Fairless and Garroni the chance to do things that wouldn’t work with solely audio. (Note: not every new podcast episode will have video.) “We grew up being obsessed with the VH1 Vogue Fashion Awards and stuff like House of Style,” says Fairless. The brilliantly lo-fi, green-screen-style opening sequence posted to their Instagram account last week distills the energy they’re going for with its nods to The Nanny, Clueless, and Access Hollywood.

Podcast listeners, TV viewers, and Instagram followers can expect new franchises like “It’s Always Fashion Week Somewhere” and “The Runway Rewind,” which will showcase the pair’s thoughts on runway shows while tapping into the tabloid entertainment vibe that they both admire. There will also be Oprah Winfrey-style book club episodes and “Top 10” lists fiercely curated by Garroni and Fairless themselves.

Ask the duo why now was the ideal time to pivot, and Fairless answers bluntly. “Lauren forced me to,” she says. Garroni sees it differently. “Chelsea finally succumbed to being on camera,” she refutes. Really, the two are responding to a general podcast-world shift to video, a medium that enables them to “fulfill an itch,” says Fairless. She didn’t have cable in her house as a child, prompting her to develop an obsession with fashion magazines and websites like First View (RIP). Garroni’s upbringing makes up for it. “My parents just gave me unrestricted access to television, cable, and the internet from a young age,” she says. Now, both of them are self-diagnosed as chronically online and cite hours on TikTok and Instagram as the reason why they collectively possess the knowledge of someone who has a PhD in fashion history.

While this wealth of niche information could potentially alienate an audience, Garroni and Fairless’s playful banter (think Siskel and Ebert, or Waldorf and Statler) makes up for it. They don’t shy away from cross-generational references, either. “We have laundered our older gay men references that we learned from watching E! News and E! True Hollywood Story,” says Garroni.

In the end, the duo intends to be authentically themselves. “I think Lauren and I are examples of millennials who are very culturally Gen X,” says Fairless. “We were always more interested in Gen X things, Gen X people. I didn’t give a shit about the Backstreet Boys when I was a teenager. We were into Hole and Pavement.”

It would be remiss not to talk about the hit television series that started it all. At this point, they have documented every outfit on Sex and the City more than once in the past ten years, but developments in the show’s universe kept them going. “Something would always happen to prevent us from abandoning this,” says Fairless. Garroni agrees, recalling when Cynthia Nixon ran for governor of New York in 2018. (They released a satirical book We Should All Be Mirandas a year later. Garroni claims to be a Miranda with a Carrie rising, while Fairless is a Miranda with a Samantha rising.) “It always sustained us,” says Garroni. “Every moment we thought, ‘Okay, how long can this joke go on for?’”

If Fairless has anything to do with it, the answer to that question is forever. “Sex and the City is never done. If there is one thing I know to be true in this life, it will never go away,” she says. “It will always change forms and there will always be something newsworthy to talk about.”

Asked what else is coming down the pipeline, Garroni is quick to mention field pieces that will take them out of their impeccably designed Los Angeles set, complete with vintage gray furniture designed in the ’90s by architect David Chipperfield and a pink carpet. (It was modeled after a mashup of Halston’s New York City apartment—an Every Outfit hyperfixation—and the Chicago department store Carson Pirie Scott.) Fairless, however, has other goals in mind. She’d like to add more single-breasted blazers to her wardrobe rotation, she says. Also: “I want hair and makeup.”

#6661. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6660. How to Plan a Trip to Easter Island, the Filming Location for ‘Wild Horse Nine’

After making a splash during the film festival circuit, director Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine has finally hit theaters. The dark comedy-thriller starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell follows two CIA operatives on their 1973 mission to the remote Pacific outpost of Easter Island. Followers of McDonagh’s work are no stranger to his interest in mind-bending landscapes (who can forget the melancholic ocean cliffs in The Banshees of Inisherin?). But the decision to shoot on Easter Island—or Rapa Nui, its indigenous name—was especially history-making.

To begin, Wild Horse Nine is not only the largest Hollywood production ever shot on Rapa Nui, but it’s also only the second. Then, of course, there are the herculean logistics of shipping period sets by boat to an island that sits more than 2,200 miles west of South America. And most critically, the crew worked hand-in-hand with local officials to coordinate filming locations that would not disrupt the archaeological sites or the sacred Rapa Nui culture. Notably, almost half of the island is part of the protected Rapa Nui National Park.

As British Vogue’s film and culture editor Radhika Seth notes, it’s a story that wins you over emotionally, and that ultimately stays with you. And if you come away from the theater with a burning desire to journey to Easter Island, let the expert-led guide below inform your 2027 travel plans.

Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, was the filming location for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine. The island sits more than 2,200 miles west of South America and is among the most remote inhabited places in the world. It is famous for its nearly 1,000 moai statues scattered across the landscape.

Rapa Nui is an island in the eastern Pacific Ocean long regarded as one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth. It is located 2,200 miles west of mainland Chile and is the easternmost outpost within the chain of Polynesian islands.

“I think there’s something incredibly special about traveling somewhere that still requires a little more effort to reach,” Carola Fresno, Timbuktu Travel’s Latin America specialist, says. Arriving by air requires a five-hour flight from Santiago, Chile, and flight connections are often limited. Because of the long-haul journey, Fresno recommends a minimum of three nights on Rapa Nui, but suggests four or five if you can swing it. “There’s so much more to the island than the famous moai statues, and it’s worth leaving time to explore properly and get under the skin of the island and the culture,” she adds.

For an oceanside stay that’s within walking distance of the island’s main town, check into Nayara Hangaroa. Each of its 75 guest rooms comes with a private terrace, and the design is driven by natural materials like cypress logs, clay, and volcanic stone. Sustainability programs go beyond the expected solar panels, extending to a local initiative that collects, recycles, and compresses and molds microplastics to transform waste material into moai figurines—a clever keepsake that reminds visitors of the importance of protecting the surrounding ocean. Guest experiences are shaped by the Hitorangi family, part-owners and cultural stewards of Nayara Hangaroa, and range from traditional dance classes and cooking demonstrations, to visits to a local beekeeper to learn why the honeybees of Rapa Nui are thought to be the world’s healthiest.

If your nationality allows you to enter Chile without a visa, one is not required for Rapa Nui. However, visitors are mandated to complete an online entry form.

It’s possible for visitors to rent a car, scooter, or bicycle to explore Rapa Nui, but many of the archaeological sites are regulated and require an accredited local guide. “Personally, I think the real value of visiting Rapa Nui lies in understanding its culture, and that’s where a knowledgeable local guide becomes invaluable,” Fresno says, who always recommends that her travelers explore with a driver and local guide.

Luxury tour operator Abercrombie & Kent partnered with Searchlight Pictures to create a Wild Horse Nine itinerary inspired by the film. “We’re seeing growing interest in film-inspired travel, particularly when a destination plays such an important role in the story,” explains A&K’s Adam Fogg, who created the itinerary. The journey begins in Santiago, discovering the events surrounding the 1973 coup highlighted in the film, eventually transporting travelers to the remote shores of Rapa Nui to explore its ancient culture and archaeology. On the island, guests enjoy dinner in a local family’s home before embarking on a nocturnal exploration. “Inspired by the legends of Haumaka and Hotu Matu'a, they discover how early voyagers crossed vast stretches of the Pacific using the stars, ocean currents, and natural elements to guide them,” Fogg says.

Beyond the film, excursions on the island range from trekking volcanic craters to horse riding up to the island’s highest point on Mount Terevaka. “One of my absolute favorite experiences is hiking along the northern coast of the island,” Fresno says. This hike showcases a quieter side of Rapa Nui and finishes at the white sands of Anakena Beach. For travelers eager to visit one of the island’s dormant volcanoes, Fresno points to a longer hike in the Poike area, which explores the volcanic landscapes and caves before continuing towards Ahu Tongariki, where 15 moai stand on a single ceremonial platform. “It’s one of the most mesmerizing sites on the island.”

If you’re a diver, the island’s volcanic origins can be explored via underwater cliffs, caves, and rock formations. “The water is this extraordinary, almost electric shade of blue,” Fresno says. “And while you won’t necessarily find the abundance of coral and marine life associated with some tropical diving destinations, the combination of exceptional visibility, volcanic scenery and the vastness of the surrounding Pacific makes diving here really special.”

Fogg notes that one of the most impactful ways to support the local community is being thoughtful about where your tourism dollars go, which includes dining at family-run restaurants. And while Rapa Nui isn’t a destination brimming with elaborate fine dining, that’s not really the point of coming here. Travelers will encounter plenty of Polynesian influences in the local cooking, as well as Chilean flavors. “I always encourage my travelers to try the seafood, particularly the tuna,” Fresno says. “The island’s isolation…is generally much more relaxed and informal, and I think that’s part of its charm.” While here, seek out an umu, which is a traditional Polynesian method of cooking food in an earth oven using heated stones.

In addition to dining at family-run restaurants and booking family-owned hotels, respecting archaeological sites and local traditions is equally important. “The island's moai and ceremonial sites hold profound spiritual and cultural significance, and visiting responsibly helps protect this extraordinary heritage,” he says.

Rapa Nui has a subtropical climate with rain throughout the year. The warmest month is February, with highs around 80 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit, while the coldest tends to be August, with lows around 59 to 63. The best time of year to visit Easter Island is between April and May and September through October when the temperatures are mild, and there are fewer tourists. If your priority is to have ideal beach conditions, consider January, February, or March (but expect bigger crowds).

#6659. Cartier Emergency? Inside the High-Stakes World of a Luxury Fashion Concierge

Private shopping appointments, last-minute deliveries, and the art of whatever the client wants.

Isn’t a fashion emergency fun when it happens to someone else? Think of the dress ripping in My Best Friend’s Wedding, or the frantic dash down Seventh Avenue in The Devil Wears Prada. These crises happen in real life, too, but are considerably less fun when they’re happening to us. How many times have you had an event and realized your look wasn’t quite right just minutes before the Uber arrives? Or stared into your suitcase on vacation wishing you had brought the espadrilles, not the sandals?

These are the sorts of requests handled by Quintessentially, the London-founded luxury concierge company that has spent the past 26 years building a business around the proposition that, for a certain class of consumer, almost anything can be arranged. Now operating in 40 cities, its U.S. operation spans private concierge services, travel, events, and guest management for luxury brands. Memberships start at $25,000 per year.

Its fashion services are particularly revealing: part cultural access and part tactical operation, run through a network of relationships built carefully over decades. Each member is assigned a lifestyle manager and a travel specialist, with a wider team of experts behind them.

“Our lifestyle managers are the lifeblood of Quintessentially,” says Lauren Wilt, U.S. CEO of Quintessentially. Many come from celebrity personal assisting, luxury hospitality, music, and entertainment—industries that reward discretion, speed, and an ability to handle big personalities. And learning the ins and outs of their clients’ idiosyncrasies is the key to their business.

“There isn’t another concierge company that gets to know their clients the way we do,” says Wilt. “This isn’t a self-service booking platform with a suite of benefits. We are a highly personalized, proactive service.”

Proactive being the operative word, and fashion offers plenty of opportunity for a lifestyle manager’s creative problem-solving. “Our members often come to us saying, ‘I’ve heard about this experience—hook me up and book it,’” said Wilt. “But it’s our job to tell them when to go, when to avoid the crowds, and sometimes that the experience they’ve seen on Instagram isn’t actually the experience for them.”

For one particularly devoted member, Quintessentially organized a Paris itinerary that was the stuff shopping dreams are made of. There were styling appointments at Dior ahead of a runway show and after-party, a private Chanel appointment arranged around a wish list submitted in advance, and lunch with Isabel Marant at her studio before attending her show. Hair and makeup were, of course, handled too. The itinerary also included a tour of vintage ateliers and heritage boutiques, with a specialist who negotiated purchases on the client’s behalf. Trop chic.

The service extends beyond the easily bookable, too. Another Quintessentially member was granted private access to Dior’s historic design archives and La Suite Dior, an invitation-only experience involving a private fragrance session, photo shoot, and a private after-hours visit to the Dior boutique. Other members have been invited into Bottega Veneta’s private New York residence, where rare and made-to-order pieces are presented alongside private dining and events.

But it’s not all about the shopping—a concierge service can also carefully curate once-in-a-lifetime experiences. When one member sought to propose to his girlfriend in Paris, Quintessentially arranged for a proposal on a flower-filled private balcony overlooking the Eiffel Tower. Afterward, the couple visited Cartier for a private appointment to choose her engagement ring together. And a surprise upgrade to the Karl Lagerfeld Suite at Hôtel de Crillon was secured.

The team also excels at solving logistical challenges. In one case, a diamond ring was collected in Geneva and delivered to a member in their suite at the Cheval Blanc Paris. And when a guest needed—truly needed—a new Saint Laurent bag and Bulgari necklace hand-delivered to their resort in the Maldives, Quintessentially made it happen.

“A brand sells you the dress; we help you with where to wear it,” Wilt says. Indeed, Quintessentially’s relationships with fashion houses operate in both directions. Luxury brands employ the company to manage the logistics surrounding their most important clients, as well as influencer trips and large-scale fashion shows and shopping events. One recent project for a fashion client involved bringing 100 couples to New York over four days, with Quintessentially coordinating car services, welcome lunches, and all the practical details that allowed the brand to focus on hosting.

But perhaps the most interesting thing about a service like Quintessentially is that it isn’t really about acquiring new things. It’s about the removal of friction, and the ability to move through the world with a degree of spontaneity. The real luxury isn’t the Birkin, the hotel suite, or the private fitting—it’s in never having to wonder how to make it all happen.

#6658. Remember When James Bond Was an Adidas Guy?

The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's getting the tux, there's another question: What sneakers is he going to wear?

As it turns out, their predecessor Daniel Craig got that bit right, too. In 2012's Skyfall, 007 turns up for his MI6 fitness tests in a navy SIS tracksuit and Adidas Gazelle IIs. In the scene, Bond's trying to prove he's fit enough to get back to work, and it's not going particularly well. As a viewer, you'd be forgiven for missing the shoes.

Daniel Craig as James Bond in Skyfall (2012).

But take another look. These were off-the-shelf Gazelles from Adidas's spring 2011 line, the sort that anyone could have picked up the year before the film came out. Bond is a guy whose wardrobe gets examined down to the last cufflink, and there he was in a regular pair of Adidas. His pair came in “dark indigo” suede with “Argentina blue” stripes, white rubber soles, and gold Gazelle lettering along the sides.

(There's a slight difference between the shoes a civilian could buy and the ones in the movie, though. The retail pair had a light blue heel tab, while Bond's appears darker. The fan website Bond Lifestyle suggests the costume department may have changed it, although that hasn't been officially confirmed.)

The Gazelle launched in 1966 as a multipurpose training shoe, and was the German sportswear giant's first-ever sneaker made from suede. The choice to put Bond in the shoe felt notable in more ways than one: In the training scene, the slim sole kept things nice and light underfoot, and the color combo went perfectly with his trackies. But there's also the Gazelle's place in British culture, from the football terraces in the ’80s to the Britpop crowd in the ’90s. So, it makes sense for a Gen-X British spy.

By 2021, Adidas had an official collab to go with No Time to Die. The collection featured all Ultraboost running shoes, with slight nods to Bond's tuxedos and Safin's porcelain mask. The “Q Branch” edition even had a hidden compartment in the lacing cage, handy if your gym shorts don't have pockets.

For a pair that came from a regular ol' Adidas collection, Bond's OG Gazelles are surprisingly difficult to find now. But if you fancy something similar without spending the next six months refreshing eBay, you can start with these.

#6657. The 6 Winter Coat Trends Defining the Season

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

From sculptural tailoring to vintage-inspired faux fur, these are the styles to know

A great winter outfit deserves an equally great coat, especially when it’s an essential layer for the next several months. Beyond the practical need for warmth, outerwear often sets the tone for an entire look as the first layer you see. A sharply tailored wool coat can make jeans and a sweater feel more polished, while an oversize silhouette or rich texture brings dimension and new proportions to otherwise clean-lined looks.

For fall/winter 2026, designers are rethinking classic outerwear through distinctive silhouettes, textures, and details. At Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi, precise tailoring took a dressier turn, with slim silhouettes, tuxedo-inspired designs, and satin lapels bringing eveningwear polish to wool coats. Meanwhile, Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry embraced leather for a sleeker city-ready take on winter dressing. Faux fur took on a distinctly vintage feel at Stella McCartney, Bottega Veneta, and Khaite, while plush collars added texture to everything from elegant overcoats to more everyday designs.

Whether you’re looking to invest in a forever piece or simply want something fresher than the coat you’ve worn for the past few winters, these six trends offer plenty of inspiration.

Faux fur is taking a distinctly retro turn this winter, with plush textures and elegant silhouettes reminiscent of vintage finds. Stella McCartney’s floor-grazing belted coat and Bottega Veneta’s voluminous fur both recall the glamour of the ’30s and ’40s, while Khaite’s shaggy cream jacket has more of a ’70s feel, particularly when dressed down with jeans. Of course, we love a faux-fur coat as the finishing touch to a dressy outfit, but there’s something even chicer about pairing one with everyday denim and boots.

Arma Verena Reversible Shearling and Leather Coat

A black coat is hardly a groundbreaking winter choice, but the fall/winter 2026 runways offered plenty of reasons for the wardrobe classic to be in focus. Designers showcased timeless silhouettes with subtle updates to keep things more interesting. Think sharp, menswear-inspired tailoring with a more formal finish at Celine or oversize cuts and dramatic lapels at Michael Kors. Tod’s introduced a different kind of drama with a sleek, draped cape design, proving that black is never boring.

Polo Ralph Lauren Wool and Silk Crepe Tuxedo Duster Coat

Favorite Daughter Metropolitan Wool and Cashmere Blend Coat

The Row Ciara Wool-Cashmere Belted Wrap Coat

There’s a certain refinement to a beautifully tailored coat, especially when the details borrow from formalwear. Think precise cuts, elongated silhouettes, and tuxedo-inspired touches that feel polished enough for an evening out. There’s a more dressed-up sensibility to these classic designs—as seen at Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi—from the precise fit to the smallest finishing details. This attention to detail brings a beautiful sense of sophistication to workwear and when paired with simple everyday separates.

Gap x Victoria Beckham Wool-Blend Chesterfield Coat

Mackage Elodie-R Double-Breasted Wool-Blend Coat

When a puffer or classic wool coat feels too predictable, a leather coat offers a much bolder alternative. Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry all embraced waist-defining silhouettes, from classic double-breasted trenches to softer robe-like shapes. In dramatic maxi lengths, the effect is especially sleek, with just the right amount of edge, bringing a bit of bite to winter dressing.

Nili Lotan Arsene Leather Double-Breasted Trench Coat

The Frankie Shop Edra Shearling-Trimmed Wrap Coat

Gray was ubiquitous on runways from New York to Paris, appearing in everything from textured tweed to draped wool and sharply tailored shapes. Whether you prefer deep charcoal or soft dove, it’s an easy neutral to wear in tonal layers or to balance bright colors and prints.

On everything from sporty puffers and classic toggle-front wool coats, as seen at Louis Vuitton, to the patterned and pretty pastel trims at Chanel and Gabriela Hearst, it’s a detail that’s as practical as it is beautiful.
